records.title: SpacePHYre: Magnetically Isolated SpaceFibre Links using Gigabit Ethernet PHYs
records.description: In this paper we present SpacePHYre, a new on-board communications CODEC that is compatible with SpaceFibre and SpaceWire networks. SpacePHYre uses magnetically isolated Gigabit Ethernet PHYs at the physical layer to provide a very high degree of electrical isolation between equipment. The magnetic isolation allows power delivery over the data cable to be supported, resulting in harness mass savings as dedicated power cabling to the equipment is no longer required. The electrical physical layer of SpaceFibre improves on the signal integrity of SpaceWire through using AC coupling to mitigate the effects of differing ground potentials and providing protection to the drivers and receivers should a DC transient fault be present on the cable. However, each end of the line is still coupled to a local ground via the discharge resistors and so this will eventually limit the length of the copper cable that can be used between two SpaceFibre devices. The AC coupling also does not fully isolate SpaceFibre devices from power supply induced transients that may occur when high-power devices are switched on or off. The fibre optic cables and drivers for SpaceFibre solve this issue but are expensive and the cables are more fragile, requiring careful handling making them less suitable for lab and AIT use. The electrical isolation can be vastly improved by moving to magnetic isolation by using a transformer between the equipment and the cable, as used in several robust interfaces such as MIL1553 and 10/100/1000BASE-T Ethernet interfaces. Space-qualified Gigabit PHY devices are becoming available on the market due to their use in Ethernet-based flight protocols, such as Time Triggered Ethernet. However, supporting the full Ethernet stack results in lots of extra features available that are not applicable to spacecraft avionics and as a consequence such avionic solution requires its own ASIC per interface as well as the physical layer PHYs and magnetics that provide the electrical isolation, the power overhead for this is many times more the SpaceFibre FPGA IP core which can be combined as part of a System-on-Chip within the same FPGA. SpacePHYre implements the SpaceFibre standard for the Network layer, Virtual Channel layer and Quality of Service provisioning. This provides the same deterministic and real-time properties of SpaceFibre links and ensures compatibility with other devices when used within a mixed SpacePHYre/SpaceFibre/SpaceWire network. The Framing and Retry layers are based on SpaceFibre, modified to support the characteristics of the Gigabit PHYs, but retain the frame formats and required frame headers to support the virtual channel and QoS provision. The Link layer presents full data or control frames to the PHY and also manages the link running state via the PHY MDIO interface or discrete signals. Control logic within the PHY handles link connection, link runtime management, as well as translation of 8-bit data words to/from tokens to be transmitted or received over the link. This removes the need for the link layer of the CODEC to manage low-level control tokens, perform 8b/10b encoding or manage the elastic buffer on the receive data path. This results in a simpler link layer when compared to SpaceFibre. SpacePHYre interfaces will complement existing SpaceFibre and SpaceWire networking by providing a significantly more robust interface, well suited to operation over long cable runs or with equipment that can generate large transients between the two endpoints. The power delivery opportunity presents large savings in harness mass and new technological development opportunities for powering remote units.

records.title: RC64: Space Manycore Enabled by SpaceWire & SpaceFibre
records.description: Abstract—RC64 rad-hard manycore DSP/ML processor employs only the Space-oriented SpFi and SpW communication protocols. It is the only known Space product fully based on these two standards. RC64 employs six SpaceWire links and twelve high-speed SpaceFibre links. This connectivity facilitates modular complex systems comprising tens and more processors spanning multiple PCBs and multiple enclosures for all Space missions. Small and reliable, thermal-cycle resilient chip packages are enabled. Systems for satellite communications, Earth observation, remote sensing, storage, cloud computing, autonomous spacecraft and instruments and more are being designed and implemented. Design considerations and challenges are described, and future versions are described. Keywords—SpaceWire, SpaceFibre, Manycore, DSP, RadHard I. RC64 ARCHITECTURE A. Processing RC64 integrates 64 DSP cores, shared memory, HW scheduler, accelerators and peripherals [Ref. AeroSpace Conf 2016 RC64 paper]. It is designed for effective and power-efficient high-performance Space applications [Ref. AeroSpace Conf 2016 DVB-S2 paper]. It has been fabricated in 2017 (65nm TSMC) and is qualified for Class Level S (300 kRad, effectively no SEL, low SEU]. It includes massive HW facilities for FDIR and Virtual Radiation Shield. B. SpaceWire Two SpW links include RMAP capabilities and enable full control by an external host processor. Four SpW links connect via DMA to the shared memory, facilitating packet networking. C. SpaceFibre Twelve high-speed serial links are included in RC64. All of them can operate as SpFi. Some can double as other protocols (SRIO). The transmit and receive parts of each link may connect to different target; for example, 12 SpFi inputs may arrive from chip X while 12 SpFi outputs are feeding into chip Y, facilitating stream processing (see below). SpFi links are managed by DMA and read from / write to shared memory. Sending and receiving SpFi data are separated in time from any processing of the data by the DSP cores. SW is used to process the data as well as to route SpFi packets and perform other Network Processor functions. II. SPW IMPLEMENTATION ON RC64 Some of the SpW links on RC64 are implemented using LVDS ports, enabling long-range and board-to-board connectivity. Other ports employ LVCMOS, saving I/O pins when intra-board connections are needed. Some standard and desirable SpW features are not implemented. Reasons will be elaborated. Radiation tests of SpW links have shown high resilience to all radiation effects. III. SPFI IMPLEMENTATION ON RC64 Ramon.Space hardened the ‘hard IP core’ SERDES ports to enhances its SEL tolerance. SEL tests demonstrated a high SEL threshold, suitable for LEO, GEO and Deep Space missions. The SERDES ports and associated ‘MAC layer’ logic enable a flexible data rate, controllable only by SW. Eye diagram and data rate tests were conducted, showing high performance up to the full 5 Gbps data rate at a wide range of cable distances. IV. RC64-BASED SYSTEM WITH AND WITHOUT A HOST A host, implemented as a CPU such as Ramon.Space GR712RC or an FPGA such as Microchip PolarFire, can be connected to the two RMAP-based ports. In fact, a ring of RC64 chips can be connected to one host, enabling resilience to any single fault. Any RC64 may boot its SW either directly from an attached boot Flash. Alternatively, it can be booted up from another RC64 chip or FPGA, through RMAP SpW. One example of a system without a host is VPX64, a single board computer based on RC64. It only boots from storage. Another example is NuStream, where RC64 may boot either from boot Flash or from a remote host, bridged through an attached FPGA. V. RC64-BASED SYSTEM USING FPGA ACCELERATION Ramon.Space single-card compute & storage product NuStream employs a Microchip PolarFire FPGA directly connected to RC64 via SpW and SpFi links. The FPGA may execute a variety of tasks such as high performance EDAC for attached 3D NAND flash units for storage. In another example, the attached FPGA performs encryption and decryptions, bit-level tasks that are more suitable for FPGA than for SW-based RC64. VI. SYSTEMS INTEGRATING MANY RC64 PROCESSORS The primary goal for a large number of SpFi (and SpW) link is to enable a dense network of many RC64 chips, capable of high-performance computations. For instance, a 2D mesh of RC64 units may be connected by channels of three SpFi links each. Note that RC64 does not implement a multi-lane protocol—data decomposition to multiple links and the corresponding assembly at the receiving end are done by SW rather than by HW cores. An alternative interconnect method implemented in RC64 splits the send and receive side of each link so that data can be pipelined over multiple stages of RC64 units, fully utilizing all links. This method is somewhat similar to JESD204B/C links typically employed in ADC and DAC products. As an example and demonstrator, a regenerative satellite transceiver was constructed where two RC64 units received ‘return channel’ data and demodulated them using DVBRCS, while two other RC64 units implemented a DVB-S2 modulator for transmitting the data to a gateway in a telecom demonstration. VII. COMPLEX SYSTEMS To be detailed in the final paper: A system comprising 5 cards, each card carrying 3x NuStream storage and processing systems and one MPSoC FPGA-based Multicore for managing card activities. VIII.NEXT GENERATION MANYCORE To be detailed in the final paper: Future generation of RC64 will extend SpFi from 12 links to 32 links, and from 5 Gbps per link to 32 Gbps per link. Some of the links will be based on Long Range SERDES enabling board-to-board high speed connectivity while other links will use Short Range SERDES, limited to on-board but dissipating much less power

records.title: SpaceFibre IP Cores for the Next Generation of Radiation-Tolerant FPGAs
records.description: SpaceFibre (ECSS-E-ST-50-11C) is a very high-performance, high-reliability and high-availability network technology specifically designed to meet the needs of space applications. It provides point-to-point and networked interconnections at Gigabit rates with Quality of Service (QoS) and Fault Detection, Isolation and Recovery (FDIR). SpaceFibre has been designed as a replacement of SpaceWire (ECSS-E-ST-50-12C) –it is backwards compatible with SpaceWire at the packet level– for next-generation space missions where very high throughput is required, providing up to 6.25 Gbit/s per lane, with multi-lane allowing to reach up to 16 times the speed of a single lane. NORBY and OPS-SAT technology demonstrators have already flown SpaceFibre, with more missions in both Europe and the USA currently designing or planning to use SpaceFibre. STAR-Dundee has developed a complete family of SpaceFibre IP cores fully compliant with the SpaceFibre standard. This family is composed of four different IPs: Single-Lane Interface, Multi-Lane Interface, Single-Lane Routing Switch and Multi-Lane Routing Switch. A new generation of radiation-tolerant FPGAs is emerging to cope with the ever-growing processing power required by newer missions. Microchip has released the PolarFire RTPF500, Xilinx the Versal XQRVC1902, and NanoXplore the BRAVE Ultra. SpaceFibre operation requires serial transceivers, which are already inbuilt in modern FPGAs. The IPs have been adapted to take advantage of the specific transceivers and memory blocks offered by these new FPGAs. In this work we analyse in detail the performance of STAR-Dundee SpaceFibre IP cores on this new generation of FPGAs considering several performance metrics, e.g. maximum lane speed, resource usage, etc. We also compare the performance of the IPs with current state-of-the-art space-grade FPGAs, i.e. Microchip RTG4 and Xilinx Kintex UltraScale XQRKU060. This analysis can also be used as a representative frame allowing to compare the performances of the different FPGAs available for space.

records.title: Simulation and hardware validation of SerDes links for SpaceFibre
records.description: The advancement of complex on-board data-handling networks constitutes a need for high-speed data links, SpaceFibre has been developed with its quality of service (QoS), fault detection, isolation and recovery (FDIR) capabilities and high data rates (up to 6.25 Gbps per lane). In 2019 a common ECSS standard has been published, which describes the basis of the protocol and its physical layer. However, a compliance testing methodology has not been described yet. Thus, this paper intends to provide a set of hardware validation and simulation-based verification strategies for SerDes links that result in best practice design guidelines. The methodologies have been evaluated with simulations and hardware tests of a FPGA-based data processing board, supporting the SpaceFibre standard on both the backplane and the front-panel connectors.

records.title: HIGH DATA RATE FLAT FLEXIBLE CABLE FOR SPACEWIRE & SPACEFIBRE
records.description: Abstract— Flat Flexible Cables (FFC) also known as Flat Conductor Cables (FCC) have many advantages and among them, a very constant geometry and robust assembly. With that in mind it makes sense to take advantage of this technology to make high data rate (HDR) connections making use of the very constant propagation time in the transmission lines. In this paper, Axon’ reviews signal integrity and EMC results from the ongoing evaluation testing of a link using a new ‘flattened’ MicroMach® connector variant dedicated to shielded FFC. This connector is based on the design of the MicroMach® SpaceWire connector ESCC3409/002. We will explore the possibility of using such media for SpaceWire and SpaceFibre compatible transmission. (Abstract) Keywords—Flat Flexible Cable, FFC, FCC, high data rate, HDR, SpaceWire, SpaceFibre (key words) I. INTRODUCTION As a manufacturer of classic Micro-D connectors and of a wide variety of round cables and interconnect used in Space, Axon’ Cable is very well versed in the pros and cons of harnesses used in harsh environments and particularly concerning EMC constraints. Axon' is also a leading manufacturer of Flat Flexible Cable commonly used in consumer electronics, office automation and automotive applications. In previous conference papers [1] [2] [3] Axon’ presented its developments in Low Mass SpaceWire cable, and also an overview of the new MicroMach® impedance-matched SpaceWire® connector development (ESCC3409/002 and ESCC3401/095 c.f. ESA contract N° 4000113741/15/NL/SW). Flexible Flat Cables (FFC) are emerging in the space sector because they offer advantages versus round wire harnesses used until now. Compared to bundles of round cable and wires, their lightness and flexibility are elements that can solve complex routing challenges. In addition, their much better heat dissipation allows higher currents to be transferred for the same cross-section of copper. II. DESIGN OF THE HIGH DATA RATE FLAT CABLE ASSEMBLY A first prototype of a Flat Flexible SpaceWire® link has been assembled using shielded flat cable and a new flat shaped connector derived from the MicroMach® design parts (see Figure 1). These connectors present 4 cavities all adapted to100Ω. This trial product opens the possibility of a new automated manufacturing solution improving flexibility and saving space. At the same time, due to the regularity features of the media skew and characteristic impedance are both significantly improved. Figure 1. Flat shaped MicroMach® connectors (inline & PCB variants) The media is based on 11 tracks of AWG28 flat conductors (0.7mm x 0.1mm); 4 differential 100Ω channels each separated by 1 track, and all encased in a 360° shielding. (See figure 2) Overall dimensions are around 1.3mm thick by 21mm wide. The signal transmission is routed over four differential stripline structures, (see Figure 3) each separated by one ground track. Figure 2. Flat Flexible Cable section Figure 3. Differential stripline structure

records.title: Hi-SIDE: Monitoring, Control and Test Software in a SpaceFibre Network
records.description: Abstract—The aim of the Hi-SIDE project [1] was to develop and demonstrate technologies that enable future high-speed on-board data-handling systems. Each of the Hi-SIDE instrument, processing and downlink elements are interconnected via the STAR-Tiger SpaceFibre [2] Routing Switch. As part of this project, software was designed and developed to monitor and control the network elements. In addition, to demonstrate the high data-rate capabilities of the processing and downlink elements in the Hi-SIDE system, software was designed and developed to support the transmission, storage, and playback of data encoded in CCSDS Space Packet Protocol [3] and Transfer Frame [4] packets at data rates of over 10 Gbit/s. This paper will describe the monitoring, control and test applications that were developed within the framework of the Hi-SIDE project and provide performance results. Keywords—SpaceFibre, Hi-SIDE, On-Board Data-Handling I. INTRODUCTION The Hi-SIDE Data-Chain (HSDC) system includes instruments to generate data; processing modules to process and compress data; a PC-based mass-memory system to store and playback data; a file-protection scheme to protect against errors or outages in optical downlinks; and optical and Ka-band downlink systems. To monitor and control the HSDC elements, the Hi-SIDE Monitoring and Control System (MCS) application was designed and developed. The MCS application provides a generic method to describe how to monitor and control elements based on the contents of the element’s RMAP [5] configuration space. Once an element is defined, its parameters can be monitored using a housekeeping service, and it can be controlled via a scripting engine. To exercise the high data-rate capabilities of the processing and downlink elements, the Hi-SIDE File Transfer applications were designed and developed. The Hi-SIDE File Transfer applications are used to encode raw files in CCSDS Space Packet Protocol and Transfer Frame packets which are then encapsulated in Hi-SIDE Payload Data or Transfer Frame encapsulation packets for routing across the SpaceFibre network. For storage and playback of data within the HSDC system, the Hi-SIDE PC-Based Mass-Memory system was designed and developed. The PC-Based Mass-Memory software provides a RAM-backed file-system capable of receiving and storing SPP packets into files and playing them back, encoded in Space Packet Protocol or Transfer Frame packets, to the processing or downlink elements at data rates of over 10 Gbit/s. The applications listed were built on top of a hardware and software stack consisting of the STAR-Ultra PCIe board and the STAR-System [6] software suite. The STAR-Ultra PCIe board provides the interface to the SpaceFibre network and includes two quad-lane ports with a lane signalling rate of up to 6.25 Gbit/s, giving a link signalling rate of up to 25 Gbit/s. Additionally, the STAR-Ultra PCIe provides multi-lane link analysis capabilities. To support the hardware, the STAR-Ultra Controller and Link Analysis applications were designed and developed. In the full paper, demonstrations and performance results of the applications listed above used within the HSDC system will be provided. ACKNOWLEDGMENT The Hi-SIDE project has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under grant agreement No 776151. REFERENCES [1] Hi-SIDE Consortium, https://www.hi-side.space/. [2] ECSS Standard ECSS-E-ST-50-11C, “SpaceFibre – Very High-Speed Serial Link”, Issue 1, European Cooperation for Space Data Standardization, May 2019, available from http://www.ecss.nl. [3] CCSDS Standard 133.0-B-2, “Space Packet Protocol”, Blue Book, Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems, June 2020, available from https://public.ccsds.org/. [4] CCSDS Standard 732.0-B-4, “AOS Space Data Link Protocol”, Blue Book, Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems, October 2021, available from https://public.ccsds.org/. [5] ECSS Standard ECSS-E-ST-50-52C, “SpaceWire – Remote memory access protocol”, Issue 1, European Cooperation for Space Data Standardization, 5 February 2010, available from http://www.ecss.nl. [6] S. Mills and S. Parkes, “A Software Suite for Testing SpaceWire Devices and Networks”, Proceedings of Data Systems in Aerospace (DASIA) Conference, Barcelona, Spain, 2015.

records.title: SystemVerilog UVM-based Verification Environment for a SpaceFibre Router
records.description: The number of space missions has seen continuous growth in the last years. Accordingly, satellite communications traffic and onboard spacecraft technologies have also increased. Hence, it was necessary to develop communication protocols capable of supporting more and more data. To manage such a high data flow, the European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) has released the SpaceFibre protocol in 2019, with support from all major international space agencies, companies and research institutes. This standard increases the capabilities of its predecessor SpaceWire, among them a higher data rate, a better Quality-of-Service (QoS), a better Fault Detection Isolation and Recovery (FDIR), and the possibility of utilizing optical fibers as communication links. One of the SpaceFibre standard’s features is that it is possible to create a Router-based Network if the data handling complexity requires it. Consequently, a crucial implementation step towards the realisation of a satellite high speed data-handling network is the design, and hence the verification, of a routing switch, with its functionalities and required compliance. However, there are no structured network-level verification environments, nor in the literature or on the market. This paper aims to propose a SystemVerilog Verification Environment based on a standard methodology, known as Universal Verification Methodology (UVM), to validate if a SpaceFibre Router is compliant with Network Layer specifications. The UVM standard is developed by Accellera, with support from multiple leading vendors, and adds features to SystemVerilog language, such as sequence, virtual sequence and data automation. The overall goals of the UVM methodology are to deliver a simple and more flexible way of creating robust test environments and make it easier to reuse verification components for new projects effortlessly and with small adjustments. A key advantage of the UVM approach is the possibility to constrain random stimuli given to the Device Under Test (DUT) easily, allowing numerous combinations of signals in a short time. This ensures control of all possible corner cases of the standard, understanding of how the DUT behaves when used out of specification, and early identification of failures in design development. The Verification Environment proposed is composed of one transmitting and one receiving agent for each virtual channel of the ports in the router. The transmitting agent is responsible for sending packets to the DUT through its driver meanwhile its monitor takes care of collecting them. Similarly, the receiving agent accumulates the incoming packets via its monitor while its driver only manages the read enable signal. All transmitting monitors send the read words to the Reference Model component, which emulates the Network Layer mechanism of the router. The Reference Model generates the expected packet based on the test stimulus and sends it to the Scoreboard component into a queue of the (port, virtual channel) tuple where it is expected to arrive. On the other hand, all receiving monitors send the collected packet directly to the Scoreboard. search_fields.title: SystemVerilog UVM-based Verification Environment for a SpaceFibre Router
search_fields.description: The number of space missions has seen continuous growth in the last years. Accordingly, satellite communications traffic and onboard spacecraft technologies have also increased. Hence, it was necessary to develop communication protocols capable of supporting more and more data. To manage such a high data flow, the European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) has released the SpaceFibre protocol in 2019, with support from all major international space agencies, companies and research institutes. This standard increases the capabilities of its predecessor SpaceWire, among them a higher data rate, a better Quality-of-Service (QoS), a better Fault Detection Isolation and Recovery (FDIR), and the possibility of utilizing optical fibers as communication links. One of the SpaceFibre standard’s features is that it is possible to create a Router-based Network if the data handling complexity requires it. Consequently, a crucial implementation step towards the realisation of a satellite high speed data-handling network is the design, and hence the verification, of a routing switch, with its functionalities and required compliance. However, there are no structured network-level verification environments, nor in the literature or on the market. This paper aims to propose a SystemVerilog Verification Environment based on a standard methodology, known as Universal Verification Methodology (UVM), to validate if a SpaceFibre Router is compliant with Network Layer specifications. The UVM standard is developed by Accellera, with support from multiple leading vendors, and adds features to SystemVerilog language, such as sequence, virtual sequence and data automation. The overall goals of the UVM methodology are to deliver a simple and more flexible way of creating robust test environments and make it easier to reuse verification components for new projects effortlessly and with small adjustments. A key advantage of the UVM approach is the possibility to constrain random stimuli given to the Device Under Test (DUT) easily, allowing numerous combinations of signals in a short time. This ensures control of all possible corner cases of the standard, understanding of how the DUT behaves when used out of specification, and early identification of failures in design development. The Verification Environment proposed is composed of one transmitting and one receiving agent for each virtual channel of the ports in the router. The transmitting agent is responsible for sending packets to the DUT through its driver meanwhile its monitor takes care of collecting them. Similarly, the receiving agent accumulates the incoming packets via its monitor while its driver only manages the read enable signal. All transmitting monitors send the read words to the Reference Model component, which emulates the Network Layer mechanism of the router. The Reference Model generates the expected packet based on the test stimulus and sends it to the Scoreboard component into a queue of the (port, virtual channel) tuple where it is expected to arrive. On the other hand, all receiving monitors send the collected packet directly to the Scoreboard. Lastly, the Scoreboard compares the received packets with the expected ones, indicating whether the test passed or failed. A peculiar aspect of the proposed solution is that it interfaces with the router via SpaceFibre Codec for each port. As a result, the Verification Environment presented can be adopted by any other Router implementation, or by another device with a SpaceFibre interface, to reduce its development and verification time by simply modifying the data-link layer connections. Thanks to the UVM methodology re-usability, all or part of the Verification Environment can be extended or included in a new project to create a more complex environment.

records.title: Evolutions of SpaceWire Protocols for Deterministic Data Delivery
records.description: Keywords—network protocols, SpaceWire, deterministic data delivery, mixed criticality systems, simulation I. ABSTRACT The primary application domain of SpaceWire networks has traditionally been payload data handling, whereas communication related to command and control has been implemented with other types of networks. Adopting a single common network for all on-board communication can lead to reduction of complexity, mass, and power demand. However, the timeliness requirements of command and control applications call for deterministic data delivery with guarantees on latency and jitter that are absent in the basic SpaceWire protocol [1]. There have been several protocols proposed that add determinism to SpaceWire, including SpaceWire-RT [2], SpaceWire-T [3], and notably SpaceWire-D [4]. The latter schedules SpaceWire traffic, defining four virtual buses of varying classes of determinism and multiplexing the traffic on them in the time domain, with time slots defined by SpaceWire time-codes sent by a network manager. The Remote Memory Access Protocol [5] is used as the transport mechanism between network nodes. This paper presents further evolutions in this area that were proposed in the ESA-funded project *SpaceDet*. Taking SpaceWire-D as the starting point, a new protocol called Mixed Criticality Message Passing protocol (MCMP), together with a new intermediate protocol for transferring data in time slots instead of RMAP, called the MCMP Register Access Protocol (MRAP), have been proposed. The mechanism for defining transmission time slots is based on local timers synchronized by a time synchronization protocol (such as the SpaceWire Time Distribution Protocol [6]), dropping direct dependence on SpaceWire time-codes. The number of available time slots in a single time epoch is thus no longer limited to 64, depending instead on a dedicated slot counter with 65536 possible values, which facilitates scheduling traffic of vastly different timing characteristics. The MRAP protocol, although based on RMAP, uses a dedicated protocol ID (so that it can be easily differentiated from RMAP) and includes protocol header optimisations, as well as extra transmission modes: unacknowledged (non-transactional) as well as raw data. Protocol features supporting FDIR have been proposed, including time slot guard margins at the beginning and at the end of a time slot, as well as using SpaceWire distributed interrupts with switches that are capable of acting on receiving them. The protocol has been implemented and tested in a network simulator. The simulation environment makes use of the MOST-X application, which is an adaptation made by Thales Alenia Space of their MOST SpaceWire simulator [7], originally based on OPNET, for the ns-3 open-source simulator [8]. MOST-X has been substantially extended in the project in order to implement the fully operational SpaceWire-D protocol as defined by the current draft specification as well as the MCMP and MRAP propositions. The test results confirmed usefulness of the proposed features of MCMP. The paper shows a subset of network simulation scenarios performed, including traffic flows of mixed characteristics of data volumes and rates, transaction frequencies, and communication patterns. records.title: Evaluation of the middle-out approach of HAYABUSA2 optical navigation system
records.description: Evaluation of the middle-out approach of HAYABUSA2 optical navigation using SpaceWire We developed a hard real-time optical navigation system based on SpaceWire-D draft standard for HAYABUSA2 asteroid probe. HAYABUSA2 was launched in December 2014 and aimed at sample-return from a near-Earth asteroid 162173 Ryugu. It completed its mission successfully in the vicinity of asteroid Ryugu in November 2019. It brought back samples of Ryugu on December 6th, 2020 to the Earth. We employed middle-out approach to integrate distributed processing elements (PEs) inside onboard computers for automatic and autonomous image recognition. Functions implemented on the distributed PEs are unified by a dedicated programming language, and the whole system can be programmed through one user programming interface. We report the evaluation result of the design approach in this paper. Digital Electronics and Optical Navigation Camera (DE-ONC) was used for scientific observation as well as for optical navigation using real-time image recognition. We developed a deterministic onboard network to fulfill the timeliness and latency requirement. SpaceWire is used both for interconnections among onboard equipment and for intra-unit connections between distributed processing elements (PEs). We referred to the design approach of parallel inference machines of the Fifth Generation Computer System, which was developed by the Institute for New Generation Computer Technology (ICOT). Thanks to the integrated architecture using SpaceWire-D, latency can be analyzed over wire harnesses and a backplane in a unit. Image tracking functions have been successfully performed during autonomous and automatic touch-down onto the surface of Ryugu. No feature points were missed, and they were tracked continuously within limited latency.

records.title: A Novel Encoding for DC-Balanced SpaceWire
records.description: Abstract— A DC-balanced encoding for SpaceWire traffic offers several advantages in flight hardware design. Conventionally, block encoding techniques have been applied to the problem. In this paper, a novel cycle-stretching method is described which takes advantage of SpaceWire’s feature of embedding clock as data. This feature allows variable-length periods to be used opportunistically to perform DC-balancing of a SpaceWire stream, without using block encoders or relying on excursions from SpaceWire protocol. Such period-adjusted encoders can show significant efficiency improvements over block encoders for randomly generated SpaceWire traffic. Look-ahead methods can be applied to further improve efficiency. An encoder whose output can be decoded by conventional SpaceWire receivers is presented. Such an encoder produces a data stream which, while being DC-balanced, can be analyzed by conventional test equipment (e.g. link analyzers) without additional hardware. The efficiency of one such encoder is analyzed using flightlike data from integration testing of Parker Solar Probe, a NASA spacecraft which uses a SpaceWire network. Candidate worst-case streams are considered. The application of this encoder for AC-Coupled SpaceWire is discussed. Keywords— SpaceWire, DC-Balanced, AC-Coupled, Encoder, Codecs.)

records.title: SpaceFibre Payload Data-Handling Network
records.description: Abstract—The Hi-SIDE project [1] is a European Union project carried out by several leading aerospace organisations from across Europe. It aims to to develop satellite data-chain technologies for future Earth observation and Telecommunication systems. Hi-SIDE has made substantial advances in the major elements of the data chain including networking, processing, compression, and downlink transmission to support the next generation of data intensive missions. The data chain elements are interconnected via a SpaceFibre network [2]. This paper introduces SpaceFibre and the Hi-SIDE project and then describes the STAR-Tiger SpaceFibre routing switch which forms the SpaceFibre network. Keywords—SpaceFibre, Payload Data-Handling, Serial Communications, Networks, Hi-SIDE I. INTRODUCTION SpaceFibre [2] is the latest generation of SpaceWire network technology for spacecraft on-board data-handling. It runs over electrical or fibre-optic cables, operates at very high data rates, and provides in-built quality of service (QoS), and fault detection, isolation and recovery (FDIR) capabilities. Because of these important characteristics, SpaceFibre was selected for use as the equipment interconnect for the Hi-SIDE project. STAR-Dundee developed the SpaceFibre interfaces for all the elements of the Hi-SIDE demonstrator along with the SpaceFibre routing switch. The STAR-Tiger SpaceFibre routing switch is the primary element of the payload data-handling network for the Hi-SIDE project [1], which is used for transferring data at high data-rates between instruments, mass-memory, data compressor/processor and downlink transmitters. It is also used to provide the control network used by the control computer to control both the network and the equipment attached to the network. The STAR-Tiger SpaceFibre routing switch has the following key features: • 10 SpaceFibre ports o Two quad-lane ports o Eight dual-lane ports o Lane speed up to 6.25 Gbit/s o Port data rate 9.6 Gbit/s (dual-lane port) • 2 SpaceWire ports • 2 further SpaceWire ports for programming STAR-Tiger • Power consumption 13.5W typical at 20 °C • 108 x 108 x 70 mm (excluding mounting brackets) • Spaceflight TRL5/6 level design o Electronic components are EM flight parts or industrial/commercial equivalents of flight parts o Conduction cooled o Operating temperature range: -25 to +55 °C Figure 1 shows a photograph of the STAR-Tiger unit. Figure 1 STAR-Tiger SpaceFibre Routing Switch In the full paper, the architecture, capabilities and performance of the STAR-Tiger routing switch will be described in detail. Its operation at the centre of the Hi-SIDE demonstration system will also be described. ACKNOWLEDGMENT The Hi-SIDE project has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under grant agreement No 776151. REFERENCES [1] Hi-SIDE Consortium, https://www.hi-side.space/ [2] ECSS Standard ECSS-E-ST-50-11C, “SpaceFibre – Very High-Speed Serial Link”, Issue 1, European Cooperation for Space Data Standardization, May 2019, available from http://www.ecss.nl

records.title: Application of SpaceWire and SpaceFibre in GR765
records.description: Abstract— The GR765 is a LEON5FT system-on-chip planned to be the successor of the GR740 quad-core LEON4FT processor. The GR740 LEON4FT quad-core processor is the highest performing LEON-based component currently available for space applications and is being applied in various missions and spacecraft architectures. The GR765 architecture includes several improvements over the GR740, most notably the addition of the LEON5FT highperformance processor that will further increase computational performance over the LEON4FT used in the GR740, while providing a low-threshold upgrade path for current GR740 users that need additional computational performance or that would benefit from the added on-chip functionality of the new architecture. Keywords—SpaceWire, SpaceFibre, SoC, fault-tolerant, RISC-V, NOEL-V, LEON, SPARC I. INTRODUCTION The LEON line of processors has a large user base within the space industry and, given the two decades of use of the LEON SPARC ISA, there is a significant amount of software heritage that can be reused. The LEON5 provides backward compatibility through implementation of the same SPARC V8(e) instruction set, adds new features to address mixedcriticality and safety-critical systems and improves computational performance. Several generations of LEON processors have included SpaceWire support, including the UT699 and UT700 LEON3FT processors and the GR712RC dual-core LEON3FT processor. The GR740 introduced an on-chip SpaceWire router, allowing users to transition from architectures that required a microprocessor and a separate router IC. The GR765 continues this trend of higher integration by increasing the number of SpaceWire ports in the on-chip router and adding support for both SpaceFibre and WizardLink. II. ARCHITECTURE The GR765 features set has a number of improvements compared to the GR740. The number of processor cores is increased from four to eight cores and the LEON5FT processor is employed instead of the LEON4FT. The LEON5FT microprocessor is a superscalar implementation that combined with improved branch prediction capabilities offers a significant performance improvement over the LEON4FT at the same processing frequency. The processor core frequency target is also increased, from 250 MHz (GR740) to 1 GHz. Doing more work per clock cycle puts additional pressure on the on-chip interconnect and on main memory systems. The GR765 will have an upgraded interconnect between the processor cores and the Level-2 cache, providing multiple parallel data paths. The primary external memory interface is currently specified as DDR2 and DDR3 SDRAM with dual x8 device correct capability. Other improvements include new dedicated DMA controllers and other interfaces such as I2C, additional SPI, MIL-STD-1553B and NAND Flash. The target technology for the implementation is STMicroelectronics 28nm FDSOI. III. SPACEWIRE AND SPACEFIBRE SUPPORT The GR740 has a SpaceWire router with eight external and four internal ports. The GR765 extends this to have twelve external ports. The current specification adds four SpaceFibre lanes supporting up to 6.25Gbit/s. These links can be reconfigured in run time to operate in WizardLink mode in order to interface equipment implementing a simpler, custom protocol. Work is ongoing to provide a hardware link between the SpaceFibre controllers and the SpaceWire router to allow communication between the different links without software intervention, as well as to add RMAP support to SpaceFibre. records.title: Eye Diagram Analyser for Space High-Speed Serial Links: a Tool for Evaluating Signal Integrity in SpaceFibre Links.
records.description: An eye diagram, or eye pattern, is a valuable metric to assess the quality of a digital signal in telecommunications. It can provide information about the link quality regarding amplitude and timing of the signal. Usually, eye diagram measuring can be performed by means of a digital oscilloscope; unfortunately, it is not always possible to assess the quality of the end-to-end communication by directly analyzing electric signals due to inconvenient electronic board pin location, layout and packaging, to the cost of adequate additional instrumentation, to the disturbance of the observed system or, most importantly, without taking into account at receiver-end aspects like equalization, additional noise and low-probability jitter. Nevertheless, the actual necessities of evaluating the quality of digital signals are increasing also in the space domain; indeed, modern and future space on board data-handling systems can require multi-gigabit communication links, and this type of measurement in high link rates is more necessary than ever. It is no wonder that private companies and also space agencies have recently adopted or developed new space-oriented high-speed protocols to fulfil the growing demand in terms of data-rate of payloads such as Synthetic Aperture Radars (SARs) and Hyper spectral imagers. Prominent examples of state-of-the-art multi-gigabit communication standards include the industry de-facto standard WizardLink or recently standardized SpaceFibre, TTEthernet and RapidIO protocols. Among them, the European Space Agency (ESA) supports the adoption of the SpaceFibre protocol, which was standardized by European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) in 2019. The SpaceFibre protocol is compatible at packet level with the well-known SpaceWire protocol, already employed in several high-profile space missions. SpaceFibre can be considered the successor of SpaceWire, drastically increasing the available link data rate from 400 Mbps to 6.25 Gbps on wire. search_fields.description: An eye diagram, or eye pattern, is a valuable metric to assess the quality of a digital signal in telecommunications. It can provide information about the link quality regarding amplitude and timing of the signal. Usually, eye diagram measuring can be performed by means of a digital oscilloscope; unfortunately, it is not always possible to assess the quality of the end-to-end communication by directly analyzing electric signals due to inconvenient electronic board pin location, layout and packaging, to the cost of adequate additional instrumentation, to the disturbance of the observed system or, most importantly, without taking into account at receiver-end aspects like equalization, additional noise and low-probability jitter. records.title: Definition, Implementation and Testing of an XML-based Packet Description Language for Traffic Analysis in a SpaceWire Communication
records.description: The on-board communication standard adopted in current generation space missions of the European Space Agency (ESA), and many other agencies as well, is SpaceWire (SpW). SpW links provide low-cost, low-latency, full-duplex, point-to-point serial links with a speed from 2 Mbit/s up to 400 Mbit/s. In a SpW network, data are exchanged as well-formed packets. A SpW packet contains a destination address, that can be composed of one or more bytes, followed by an unlimited-length packet cargo that ends with a special End-Of-Packet (EOP) character. This structure offers low packet overhead and allows developers to easily tailor their implementation for specific applications. Although the SpW packet format, defined in ECSS-E-ST-50-12C standard, is flexible and easy to implement, it originally lacked a mechanism for packet identification and reuse. For this reason, a new packet format has been defined by the SpW working group as an extension of the existing SpW packet format, adding a "Protocol ID" field as the first byte of a packet cargo. This has allowed the definition of several protocols, such as the Remote Memory Access Protocol (RMAP) or the CCSDS Packet Transfer Protocol, that can be easily deployed in different SpW applications. This paper presents the definition of the SpW Packet Description Language (SpW PDL), based on the eXtensible Markup Language (XML), to provide SpW developers with an instrument to easily define SpW packets, in both human-readable and machine-readable manner, aiding in the development of packet-format independent SpW applications. As a matter of fact, the adoption of the SpW standard requires the verification of compliance with the standard itself. For this reason, it is critical to dispose of a set of tools and instrumentation to test SpW applications and SpW-based systems. Such test-equipment is part of those systems referred to as Electrical Ground Support Equipment (EGSE). Nonetheless, while testing SpW-based systems, it is crucial to verify not only the correct operation of SpW Interfaces but also the transmission/reception of correct data, i.e., the SpW packet formatting and flow. For this reason, the SpW PDL has been integrated into the SpaceART SpaceWire Sniffer, a user-friendly SpW link analyzer, designed to unobtrusively test and verify SpW communication between two SpW nodes. This work not only provides the definition of the SpW PDL but also describes how it has been integrated into the SpaceART SpaceWire Sniffer, to efficiently inspect SpW traffic, seeking specifically formatted SpW packets. The SpW PDL allows the developer to simply define a single, or a set of, SpW packet structures by means of an XML file, adhering to a specifically designed XML schema. Such XML file can then be used by specific software for testing SpW-based systems. This is the case of the SpaceART SpaceWire Sniffer, in which the XML description of a SpW packet can be used to explore SpW data traffic, seeking the occurrence of that specific packet. A test-scenario representing a SpW communication based on RMAP protocol is also presented, proving the capability of the SpaceART SpaceWire Sniffer, for analyzing transmitted data, and the potential of the SpW PDL for parsing such data, matching RMAP SpW packets. The present work comprises five sections: at first an introduction about EGSE, SpW Standard and SpW packet format is given, introducing also SpW Protocol ID and RMAP protocol. Then the SpW PDL is presented, describing its definition and implementation. Later on, the SpaceART SpW Sniffer is described followed by a use-case scenario in which it is used to analyse SpW traffic, exploiting the SpW PDL. In conclusion, the result of the use of such technologies is given.

records.title: SPACE-GRADE 1-10 GBPS PARALLEL OPTICS TRANSCEIVERS AND PARALLEL OPTICAL CONNECTORS FOR SPACEFIBRE DATALINKS
records.description: We report on development and qualification testing of space-grade high-speed parallel fiberoptic transceivers and mechanical transfer (MT) optical connectors to support SpaceFibre fiber-optic data networks on-board spacecraft. The transceivers employ hermetically sealed opto-electronic hybrid circuits and low-loss optical coupling that provide optical link performance conforming to the requirements of the SpaceFibre physical layer standard at data rates up to 10 Gbps. The transceivers have undergone extensive environmental and radiation testing including shock and vibration, as well as proton, heavy ion and gamma exposure tests. Ruggedized MT parallel optical connectors were also developed in rectangular and circular formats suitable for spacecraft applications. Taken together, these products enable rapid deployment of the optical physical layer of the SpaceFibre standard. This brings full realization of the substantial mass reduction possible when replacing heavy SpaceFibre copper cables with extremely light-weight all-dielectric optical fibre cables. The use of optical fibre also greatly extends the distance possible for transmission of 10 Gbps signals, compared to copper SpaceFibre copper cables, due to elimination of the coax cable attenuation losses. The intrinsically light weight of the optical fibres, and the lack of metallic shielding typically required for EMI/RFI reduction, as well as the elimination of many grounding and ground-loop issues, bring substantial weight-reduction benefits to spacecraft datalinks. We present results detailing the construction, environmental testing, radiation exposure tests and thermal and reliability analysis for these modules and optical connectors. The results show that these extremely high-density transceivers and fibre-optic connectors meet or exceed many of the requirements of spacecraft applications and can be employed to enable optical SpaceFibre links onboard spacecraft.

records.title: SpaceWire hardware abstraction layer Considerations
records.description: The software development for spacecraft is required to be faster while ensuring reliability, such as mass production and shorter development turnaround time. The methods to improve the efficiency in software development include the formulation and implementation of software platforms and the standardization of onboard data communication applications. And it has been discussed and specified by CCSDS SOIS (Spacecraft Onboard Interface Services Area), and communication middleware and platforms have been developed. On the other hand, hardware designs are constantly being updated for higher speed, higher functionality, and higher reliability. The hardware design changes and procurement of devices from multiple companies result in not only driver updates but also software interface changes between the drivers and middleware. In spacecraft development, model-based, simulation, and target-hardware board development are conducted for each process, so the development and verification using a combination of middleware and actual board drivers are backward processes. Therefore, this study examined the SpaceWire hardware abstraction layer that can be used with multiple actual target boards and middleware. In addition, we developed and verified an abstraction layer driver that can be used with various middleware and host OSs to validate.

records.title: A Generic SpaceWire Transport Layer
records.description: Abstract The transport layer is the essential part in the open system interconnection (OSI) reference model [1], since it is the interface between the software-oriented layers 5-7 and hardware- oriented layers 1-3. On the one hand, it provides a general approach for data exchange with the software-oriented layers, independent of underlying hardware [2]. On the other hand, it is responsible for an efficient and reliable use of the underlying hardware [2]. These characteristics make the transport layer that important for the usage of a communication system, since it reduces the implementation effort for the software-oriented layers significantly. The lack of a transport layer is a huge disadvantage. Com- bining the functionality of the different communication layers in single application specific protocols not only leads to the coexistence of several non compatible approaches. This also leads to a higher implementation effort for the integration of new applications. Therefore, the existence of a transport layer is fundamental for both, to provide established communication concepts, which are a precondition for the use of standardized software libraries, and to integrate modern computing trends (e.g. Big Data, Data-Mining, machine learning, cyber security). SpaceWire does not yet define a general transport layer. This paper presents the approach of a minimalist transport layer, as common base for the implementation of higher level protocols. It comprises both the hardware related SpaceWire transport node and the associated software counterpart as well as the associated protocol. The transport layer implementation is one result of our longstanding SpaceWire development and is already in use in several robotic systems. Index Terms—SpaceWire transport level, transport layer, robotic I. I NTRODUCTION According to the OSI reference model the transport layer has two tasks [2]. First, to provide a generic interface to the upper layers to initiate data transfers. The specific details of the lower layers are hidden and only services for connectionless and connection-oriented communication are provided. Hence, from the upper layer point of view the data transfer is completely hardware independent. Second, initiated data transfers have to be performed in an efficient and reliable manner under consideration of the given lower layers. Therefore, the transport layer has to establish a connection between a source and a destination, perform the data transfer (which is implemented as send and/or receive of a dedicated number of packets over the network) and closing the connection after completion. Whereas the closing can be optional in case of a permanent connection between two peers. To achieve these tasks a minimalist SpaceWire transport layer has to provide the following issues: • A configuration mechanism to establish a connection between two nodes. • A SpaceWire transport layer configuration protocol in- cluding error detection. • SpaceWire transport nodes for connectionless (datagram) and connection-oriented (request/response) communica- tion. • A SpaceWire transport layer protocol for datagram and request/response including error detection. This paper introduces a minimalist SpaceWire transport layer and its components. Section II defines a SpaceWire transport layer protocol for the configuration of connections as well as for datagram and request/response communication. Based on this protocol, a Very High Speed Integrated Circuit Hardware Description Language (VHDL) implementation of a generic SpaceWire transport node for connectionless and connection-oriented communication is presented in Section III. Section IV gives an overview of the associated software representation of the SpaceWire transport layer. The paper concludes in Section V with the findings regarding the usage of the SpaceWire transport layer in our robotic systems and outlook to possible extensions. REFERENCES [1] Dimitrios Serpanos and Tilman Wolf. Architecture of network systems. Elsevier, 2011. [2] Andrew S Tanenbaum et al. Computer networks, 4-th edition. Prentice Hall, 2003.

records.title: The Communication Infrastructure of TINA, a Space Robot for Sample Return Missions
records.description: Abstract This Is Not an Arm (TINA) is a modular torque con- trolled robot for sample return missions [1]. With SpaceWire [2] as the quasi official standard for on board data communication of spacecrafts and satellites its usage in involved components like e.g. robots is reasonable. Apart from the compatibility aspect, SpaceWire’s features especially its determinism and time distribution approach fit well to robotic demands. This could be showed in several terrestrial applications [3]–[8]. Hence, using SpaceWire as the communication backbone for TINA is the obvious choice. About 20 years development of SpaceWire based robots shows, a view enhancements to the existing SpaceWire stack are necessary to completely fulfill the requirements given by a robotic system. Beside, a adapted physical level providing Gb/s data rate for main control loop frequencies up to 10 KHz [9], a transport level approach is most important to support common software paradigms like request/response and datagram [6], [7]. However these important and convenient enhancements are contradict to the existing SpaceWire standard. Therefore TINA follows a two pronged approach with two parallel topologies. One based on the developed enhancements the other one fully standard conform. This enables both, debugging, testing and setup of the normal operation with the enhancements and if desired normal operation via the standard SpaceWire protocol on packet level. Index Terms—TINA, space robotics, communication infras- tructure, SpaceWire I. INTRODUCTION As TINA is a space robot the development banks on highly reliable and established methods and components to meet the strong requirements existing for hardware in space. This is also relevant for the used communication system and the associated protocols. As a consequence, the standard SpaceWire stack and its existing protocols should be used. Unfortunately, a seamless integration of the standard SpaceWire stack, including its protocols into modern middleware and hardware abstraction layer approaches is not possible due to the lack of an transport level. A transport level hides hardware related issues to the upper levels and simply provides standard communication paradigms like request/response and datagram for data ex- change [10]. This eases debugging, testing and also changes during normal operation as well as supports reusability of software due to the hardware independence. These aspects are important at the development process of a robot. All of our so far SpaceWire base developed robots [3], [4], [6], [11] profit from this approach. To overcome this conflict between standard conformity and easing of software development and the development process, both approaches are implemented in parallel. As a result, data exchange can either be performed on transport level or on packet level within the standard SpaceWire stack and protocols. This paper introduces the SpaceWire communication infras- tructure of the space robot TINA. Section II gives an overview of the overall communication concept. The SpaceWire capa- bility on joint level and the different usable topologies are described in Section III. Section IV deals with the associated control software and their integration into the SpaceWire topology. The paper concludes in Section V with the results of the integration process. records.title: SPACEMAN 2: Towards Multi Protocol Network Management
records.description: Keywords—network management, NDCP, SpaceFibre, SpaceWire I. ABSTRACT In response to increasingly ambitious goals for future space missions and the associated needs of higher on-board data communication rates and quality, initiatives are on-going to upgrade the current communication technologies and add new services, for instance through the development of SpaceFibre or the adoption of Ethernet-based ground technologies. The complexity of the resulting networks and protocols calls for appropriate measures for management. For SpaceWire such a measure was introduced in the form of the Network Discovery and Configuration Protocol (SpW NDCP) [1]. One of the first implementations of SpW NDCP together with a network management application called SPACEMAN was delivered by ITTI in a project for ESA [2,3]. The SPACEMAN application originally supported SpaceWire Networks composed of NDCP-aware Devices and non-NDCP aware SpW-10X routing switches. Evolution of the application continued so as to support the new protocols and new Device models, as well as enable cooperation with other applications. The paper presents the results of that progress which found their place in the revised SPACEMAN 2 application or are being developed, within the frame of the ESA-funded project *Multi-Protocol On Board Communications Network Manager*. The major development direction is the support of more network protocols, beginning with SpaceFibre. In order to achieve this, the original SpW NDCP had to be extended into a new version, described in a companion paper [4], with SpaceWire support retained though modified. Compatibility across versions is maintained: SPACEMAN 2 can handle both versions of NDCP. Pure SpaceWire or SpaceFibre as well as mixed SpaceWire/SpaceFibre Networks are supported. The next network technology for which support is being developed is IEEE 802.1-based Time Sensitive Networking. Since NDCP support in commercially available Devices is still scarce, SPACEMAN is continuously expanded to handle more non-NDCP aware device models via RMAP [5]. In addition to the originally supported SpW-10X routing switch and compatible Devices it can now handle STAR-Dundee SpaceFibre Devices (like the STAR Fire or the SpaceWire and SpaceFibre Router) and Shimafuji SpaceWire Router. Support of Gaisler GR718B 18x SpaceWire Router is under way. Devices are also being added to the range of supported “management gateways”, i.e. Nodes through which SPACEMAN connects to Networks managed; these include now TELETEL iSAFT boards, STAR-Dundee PCI boards and USB-equipped bricks and routers, and Shimafuji routers. The management gateways can also be accessed remotely over TCP/IP. The paper describes the differences between network management using NDCP, with well-defined standardised parameters, and using RMAP, where parameter sets, memory layouts, and addressing modes differ across the device range, and where parameters crucial for Device identification and Network topology discovery may be missing, requiring workarounds. The different organisations of Device parameters are represented in SPACEMAN 2 as Device data models. Several Network discovery modes are presented, with responsibility of detecting the appropriate Device data model shared differently between the application and the user, from fully automatic, through user-guided, to manual. Facilities for cooperation of SPACEMAN 2 with other application are shown, both on-line via TCP/IP, like including accessing remote managed Networks, exchanging Network models at runtime, or connecting to a network simulator, and off-line via the file system, like exporting or importing Network models and packet definitions. Various innovations in user interaction possibilities are presented. If possible, some of them will be shown as a short video embedded in the presentation. records.title: Qualification of One and Two Connector Disconnects in a Spacewire Link for a GEO Space Robotics Servicer
records.description: Abstract— Hundreds of government and commercial satellites reside in geosynchronous Earth orbit (GEO) some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) above the Earth—an ideal location for providing critical services and information, but effectively inaccessible for repair or upgrade. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s (DARPA’s) Robotic Servicing of Geosynchronous Satellites (RSGS) program intends to change that dynamic by developing technologies that enable cooperative inspection and servicing in GEO. The RSGS robotic servicing vehicle, consisting of a robotic payload developed by the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) and a space vehicle bus developed by a commercial partner, intends to demonstrate those technologies on orbit within the next five years. To accomplish this mission, the RSGS robotic payload needs to integrate data from and send commands to situational awareness cameras, inspection cameras, remote command and telemetry boxes, rendezvous/proximity operation sensors, payload control computers and the spacecraft bus. SpaceWire enables the many disparate components of the robotic payload to talk to each other in a robust and reliable way, and was an ideal choice as the backbone of our communications network. In order to simplify integration and test, connector disconnects were requested in the SpaceWire cabling connecting these components. NRL has validated non-standard cabling previously as documented in a paper for the 2008 International SpaceWire conference and applied that knowledge to qualify these non-standard cables. NRL built three four-meter long test cables with zero, one and two series 79 connector pairs inline. These cables were subjected to a test campaign over temperature including time domain reflectometry, insertion loss measurement, bit error rate testing, link rate testing and eye diagram analysis. The test campaign, test equipment and pass/fail criteria are provided as a notional qualification procedure for future non-standard cables. All test results in all test configurations passed at 200Mbps with significant margin. The test results show an expected trend in that the cable with no connections is better than one in-line connection cable which is better than the cable with two inline connections. There was a slight trend in results over temperature in that results at hot temperature are better than test results at ambient temperature which is better than results at cold. The effects are much less impactful than expected in that no measurement deviated more than fifteen percent across all configurations, and all temperatures.

records.title: STP-ISS Assessment in Deterministic Spacewire Network with ESA MOST Spacewire Simulator
records.description: ABSTRACT- SpaceWire is a protocol developed for space use and specifically for Spacecraft. Its numerous advantages enable a wide use in the space industry in particular comparing to the well-known MIL-STD 1553 bus. In fact it is a low cost, low consumption and high data rates communication link which can even be used for a network. ISS-Reshetnev has developed a specific standard which brings some mechanisms for providing some Quality of Service (QoS). Using these QoS in a network, this can bring a high level of determinism on the spacecraft for a good equipment and behavior management. This paper aims to explore and comment the STP-ISS by implementing this additional Spacewire layer on a Simulator based on NS3.

records.title: SpaceWire Codec VIP: an innovative architecture of UVM-based Verification Environment
records.description: SpaceWire (SpW) devices are widely used in space applications on-board satellites. Their verification is fundamental because it ensures that the Design Under Test (DUT) is bug-free, without the risk of compromising an entire space mission. In this paper an innovative architecture of a Verification IP (VIP) based on Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) for the testing of a SpW Codec IP core is presented. It is based on a Twin Model, developed in SystemVerilog Hardware Verification Language (HVL), which emulates the ideal behavior of the SpW Codec. The Twin Model internal structure reflects the layered one that UVM standard suggests using for the development of Verification Environments, with significant advantages in terms of reusability and maintainability. It can communicate directly with the DUT and, more in general, with any SpW device, through the Data-Strobe interface. The advantages of the Twin Model are exploited by implementing a direct communication between it and the DUT, allowing the user to manage the sending and receiving of information data only. In fact, the SpW protocol requires the continuous exchange of additional data between two nodes for the creation and maintenance of the communication link. The Twin Model is able to autonomously send it, relieving the user of this task. The proposed architecture leverages the Twin Model advantages in an additional way: a secondary communication link, named Twin Link and connecting two Twin Models, is added in parallel with the principal one. The Twin Link emulates the ideal communication link behavior, similarly to the Twin Model for the SpW Codec IP core. It is used for the verification of specific simulation scenarios, such as the management of any error by one of the two SpW nodes (Disconnect, Parity error, ESC error, Credit error etc..). These are injected by a specific functional block that intercepts, recognizes and corrupts the data traffic on Data-Strobe interface. It is able to inject both random and user-defined errors. Without the Twin Link, the user should manually describe the expected behavior of the communication link to compare it with the actual one. With this architecture the VIP replicates on the Twin Link both input stimuli and errors defined for the main link; then it automatically compares if both data and broadcast codes transmission and error handling are performed in the same way on the two links. The result is a highly reliable and configurable VIP that allows for automated testing of all functionalities of any SpW codec. In addition, due to the full UVM compliance of both the Twin Model and the verification environment, both can be reused in other IP verification projects involving SpW interfaces. The high efficiency of this VIP leads to a substantial reduction in verification time and effort.

records.title: SpaceWire Routing Simulator for Distributed Computing Systems Using OMNeT++
records.description: Improvements in satellite technology and manufac- turing have given engineers access to new possibilities in satellite design. Lower costs of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) com- ponents allow for a more cost-effective spacecraft development, while increasingly accessible launch services allow for higher volumes of spacecraft to be launched than ever before. These new options and possibilities create a very large trade-space to be explored during the design process, where engineers must ensure that the components can fulfill the mission’s requirements. One key aspect is the on-board communication. Due to the sharing of information between instruments, processing units, and other components of the spacecraft, the selection of a network and its topology can significantly affect the overall performance. Any large delays in data transmission may interfere with the execution of tasks or lead to outdated information. SpaceWire provides an effective communication network with wormhole routing. This allows for minimal buffer size in the routers, while providing low latency. However, this protocol is susceptible to delays whenever two incoming messages need to use the same outgoing port of a router. In this case, one message has to wait until the other has finished its transmission, thereby blocking all ports that it is occupying, and possibly causing a cascade of blocking throughout the network. This is especially relevant in networks where all nodes are connected to a central node that acts as a hub for the rest of the network. It is therefore essential to consider the design of the network in conjunction with the on-board applications when designing a spacecraft. Although models can be used to estimate delays and network utilization, a simulator provides a deeper insight into its behavior. This paper presents a simulator of SpaceWire networks, created in OMNeT++, which can be used to test different network and application architectures for satellite missions. In this simulator, the network consists of the processing components and routers. Each component generates messages either peri- odically or in response to the incoming messages. The routers then transmit the messages, following the SpaceWire protocol. Messages are forwarded one bit at a time and stored in the routers’ buffers. If a buffer reaches its capacity, the message stops being received until the buffer has free space. During these pauses, the outgoing buffer in the sender router also stops transmitting and stores the remaining bits until it can resume the transmission. This simulates the behavior of a SpaceWire network with wormhole routing, and can be used to track the activation of tasks, the transmission times for each message, and network utilization. This short paper also shows a series of examples that demon- strate the applicability of the simulator as a useful tool that can aid engineers and system developers to better assess any future designs.

records.title: SpaceWire Test and Development with STAR-System and the SpaceWire PCIe Mk2
records.description: *Abstract*—Although SpaceWire [1] is fast approaching its 20th anniversary, the requirements for equipment to test and develop new SpaceWire devices and networks continues to evolve and push the capabilities of commercial technology. STAR-Dundee has developed a new PCI Express product, the SpaceWire PCIe Mk2, to take advantage of the higher data rates offered in newer generations of the PCIe standard. The device features three SpaceWire ports capable of operating at 400 Mbit/s link speeds, and the PCIe Gen-3 interface enables transmitting and receiving at the maximum rate on all links concurrently. This high throughput is made possible through improvements to the STAR-System software suite [2], which also includes other new features to support the latest requirements for SpaceWire test and development. As well as new graphical applications providing functionality such as the ability to operate as an RMAP [3] initiator, support for ARM targets and the Python scripting language are also included. This paper will describe the advancements present in the SpaceWire PCIe Mk2 board and the STAR-System software suite, which simplify test and development activities while also providing higher throughput and lower latency transmission and reception of data. *Keywords—SpaceWire, Test and Development, SpaceWire PCIe Mk2, STAR-System* I. INTRODUCTION The requirements for SpaceWire test and development products continue to evolve as the functionality offered by commercial technology changes. Back in 2002, a SpaceWire PCI board with ports operating at 200 Mbit/s, offering a maximum throughput of 800 Mbit/s to a 32-bit x86 Windows XP PC and accessed via a C API, was a perfectly good solution for testing new SpaceWire developments. In 2022, 400 Mbit/s SpaceWire links are sometimes required, while PCIe Gen-3 offers the capability to transfer data to and from all three of the SpaceWire ports on STAR-Dundee’s new PCIe board, the SpaceWire PCIe Mk2, at the full 400 Mbit/s data rate on each port, giving a total throughput in excess of 1.9 Gbit/s. The host computers have also evolved, and STAR-Dundee’s latest STAR-System software suite supports both Windows and Linux on 32-bit and 64-bit x86 machines, with ARM targets also supported on Linux. The C programming language continues to be popular but newer scripting languages such as Python simplify the implementation of test scripts, while graphical applications to perform common tasks can potentially eliminate the need for any development using an API in some scenarios. The latest version of STAR-System includes C, C++ and Python APIs plus several new graphical applications to perform tasks such as configuring deterministic triggering behaviour and acting as an RMAP initiator. In the full paper, throughput and latency performance charts for the SpaceWire PCIe Mk2 will be provided, the extensive fault protection included in the board will be described and the deterministic capabilities offered by the board’s external triggers will be explained. search_fields.title: SpaceWire Test and Development with STAR-System and the SpaceWire PCIe Mk2
search_fields.description: *Abstract*—Although SpaceWire [1] is fast approaching its 20th anniversary, the requirements for equipment to test and develop new SpaceWire devices and networks continues to evolve and push the capabilities of commercial technology. STAR-Dundee has developed a new PCI Express product, the SpaceWire PCIe Mk2, to take advantage of the higher data rates offered in newer generations of the PCIe standard. The device features three SpaceWire ports capable of operating at 400 Mbit/s link speeds, and the PCIe Gen-3 interface enables transmitting and receiving at the maximum rate on all links concurrently. This high throughput is made possible through improvements to the STAR-System software suite [2], which also includes other new features to support the latest requirements for SpaceWire test and development. As well as new graphical applications providing functionality such as the ability to operate as an RMAP [3] initiator, support for ARM targets and the Python scripting language are also included. This paper will describe the advancements present in the SpaceWire PCIe Mk2 board and the STAR-System software suite, which simplify test and development activities while also providing higher throughput and lower latency transmission and reception of data. *Keywords—SpaceWire, Test and Development, SpaceWire PCIe Mk2, STAR-System* I. INTRODUCTION The requirements for SpaceWire test and development products continue to evolve as the functionality offered by commercial technology changes. Back in 2002, a SpaceWire PCI board with ports operating at 200 Mbit/s, offering a maximum throughput of 800 Mbit/s to a 32-bit x86 Windows XP PC and accessed via a C API, was a perfectly good solution for testing new SpaceWire developments.
