records.title: Properties of electrons accelerated during the Galilean moons-magnetosphere interaction : survey of Juno high latitude observations
records.description: In Jupiter's magnetosphere, the Galilean moons disrupt the flow of magnetodisc plasma driven in quasi-corotation by the planet's magnetic field. This interaction gives rise to a variety of physical processes, including the generation of Alfvén waves that can propagate along magnetic field lines and accelerate charged particles. One manifestation of these phenomena is the parallel acceleration of electrons that precipitate into Jupiter's atmosphere, triggering UV auroral emissions. These auroral footprints are composed of a main spot, the Main Alfvén Wing (MAW) spot followed by an auroral tail that extends in the direction of the magnetospheric plasma flow. Depending on the location of the moons in the Jovian magnetodisc, a spot created by a Trans-hemispheric Electron Beam (TEB) The Juno spacecraft, in orbit since 2016, allows to characterize in-situ the particles accelerated during the moon-magnetosphere interactions thanks to its highly inclined orbit. In-situ measurements obtained within the magnetic field lines connecting the moons' orbital locations to Jupiter's atmosphere reveal the diversity of physical processes occurring during the moon-magnetosphere interactions. We present here a comparison of the properties of electrons measured in the Io-, Europa-, and Ganymede-Jupiter circuits by Juno. In particular, we explore the energy distributions and show that different distributions are observed. At all three moons, electrons creating the MAW spot and the auroral tail always have broadband distribution while in the TEB flux tubes of the two moons that Juno has crossed, Europa and Ganymede, the electrons are distributed non-monotonically, with a higher characteristic energy. This observation provides an important insight for the study of particles acceleration processes involved in the moon-magnetosphere interactions.

records.title: Satellite Microsignatures in Jupiter's Radiation Belts
records.description: The term "microsignatures" refers to localized decreases in trapped particle flux caused by particle absorption by moons or rings that orbit within a planetary magnetosphere. Microsignatures can survive for hours and thus propagate far from the parent moon and its magnetospheric interaction region. They thus evolve under the influence of the background magnetospheric environment, meaning that their profile and location can trace processes in the magnetosphere itself, such as particle transport. Microsignatures are most common in electrons from few keV and up to the ultra-relativistic range (>10 MeV). A large number of microsignature detections at Saturn has revolutionized our understanding of energetic particle transport processes in the planet's radiation belts. However, to this date, we lack a comprehensive survey of satellite microsignatures at Jupiter, even though few single case studies demonstrate their detectability in both the Galileo and Juno datasets. To proceed with their detailed study at Jupiter, it is necessary to first develop a framework that allows us to predict their timing and verify under which conditions, geometries and energies such predictions are most successful. The complex magnetospheric configuration at Jupiter (compared to the spin-aligned magnetic field of Saturn) introduces several challenges. In this work, we present the first steps towards developing this framework and contrast our initial predictions against energetic particle observations by Galileo and Juno. We show that microsignatures are present even in low-time resolution measurements of Galileo/EPD. In the Juno/JEDI dataset, we find microsignatures from most Galilean moons, as well from smaller, asteroid-sized moons in the inner belts (e.g. Metis). We further extrapolate our predictions for the JUICE mission and show the long-residence of JUICE in the inner magnetosphere, particularly close to the orbits of Ganymede and Callisto, would result in unique geometries and opportunities to probe Jupiter's inner and middle magnetosphere with microsignature observations.

records.title: Periodic narrowband radio wave emissions and inward plasma transport at Saturnian magnetosphere
records.description: The abrupt brightening of an Energetic Neutral Atom (ENA) blob or cloud has been interpreted as plasma injection in the Saturnian magnetosphere (termed ENA injection herein). Morphologically, there appears to be two types of abrupt ENA cloud brightening: (1) the brightening of a large cloud usually seen at distances > 10-12 Rs (Rs = 60,268 km) in the midnight or postmidnight region; (2) the brightening of a smaller cloud usually seen at distances < 10-12 Rs around 21-03 magnetic local time (MLT). Among many radio waves observed at Saturn, type 2 ENA injections correlate best with the 5 kHz narrowband waves. Using Cassini INCA and RPWS data, we examine the periodicities of the type 2 ENA injections and the 5 kHz narrowband emissions as well as their cross-correlations, which have been previously used to measure the lag times or phase differences. Because correlational analysis can only establish linear relationships, we also use mutual information to establish linear and nonlinear relationships. On average, the peak of the 5 kHz narrowband emission lags those of the type 2 ENA injection by a few minutes to 2 hr. The injection of hot plasma to the inner magnetosphere can lead to temperature anisotropy, which can generate electrostatic upper hybrid waves, which upon encountering the density gradient at the outer edge of the Enceladus plasma torus, can mode convert to the Z mode and then to O mode. The 5 kHz narrowband waves commonly propagate in the O mode.

records.title: Moon-magnetosphere interactions in the outer solar system
records.description: Our current understanding of the moon-magnetosphere interactions is primarily based on the analysis of of data obtained during past and current missions to the outer solar system. In addition, telescope observations of giant planets and their moons allowed us to gain new knowledge and think more deeply about issues from many different perspectives. In parallel, theoretical progress in the field of space plasma physics and numerical simulations have significantly contributed in our better understanding of the near-moon environments and the underlying physical processes as well as their variability both at long and short terms. The various moon environments in the outer solar system are in general different depending both on the bodies properties and the specific characteristics of the planetary magnetosphere in which they are embedded. Although each case of moon-magnetosphere interaction is unique, a comparative planetary science context can often result useful in our overall understanding of the related physical processes. Among others, Ganymede’s interaction with its surrounding plasma environment is of special interest, mainly because this moon possesses its own mini-magnetosphere. Reconnection allows Jovian plasma and energetic ions to access the moon’s surface where they precipitate following patterns that depend on the position of Ganymede with respect to the Jupiter plasma sheet. An in depth understanding of the properties of the plasma-magnetosphere interactions in the vicinity of Ganymede will reveal the details determining the ion-surface processes responsible for the exosphere generation as well as the weathering and the surface evolution history. In this talk I will briefly discuss some paradigms of moon-magnetosphere interactions in the outer solar system with special emphasis to the unique case of Ganymede. The role of comparative science in getting the global picture and addressing long-lasting open questions in this field will be also addressed.

records.title: Electrons near Europa and in fluxtubes magnetically connected to Europa’s footprint tail aurora at Jupiter
records.description: The interactions of the Jovian moons and Jupiter’s magnetosphere create fascinating auroral emissions at the moons and Jupiter. The emissions are the visible result of electron-impact excitation of the atmosphere that are caused by precipitating electrons which are accelerated from those interactions. Juno’s trajectory crossed multiple times fluxtubes that are magnetically connected to the auroral footprint tails of the moons near Jupiter. And later in its extended mission, Juno also flew near Ganymede, Europa, and Io. In this presentation, we summarize the plasma observations near Jupiter and the moons, with a focus on Europa. In particular, the Jovian Auroral Distributions Experiment (JADE) observed magnetic field-aligned electron beams near Europa. The energy and location of these beams are critical factors in better understanding Europa’s space environment, as the beams are predicted to have an outsized influence on the ionization of the constituents of Europa’s atmosphere and are accompanied with large magnetic field perturbations. The beams therefore play an essential role in shaping Europa’s space environment and affect future attempts to diagnose Europa’s interior.

records.title: Revisiting Galileo Flybys to Constrain Europa's Subsurface Ocean
records.description: Jupiter's icy moon Europa is a primary target for the study of ocean worlds. Its subsurface ocean's salinity (electrical conductivity), thickness, and depth are not well constrained and still subject of current research, over twenty years after the Galileo mission. In this study, we revisit a selection of Galileo's Europa flybys suitable for the study of the ocean's induced magnetic field. Using the PLUTO code to solve the three-dimensional MHD equations, we model plasma interactions between the Jovian magnetosphere and Europa's atmosphere with the aim to obtain a better understanding of both Europa's subsurface ocean (depth and conductivity) and its neutral O$_2$ atmosphere.

records.title: Exploring Titan's Complex Plasma Interactions: Proposed Payload for the Dioscuri Space Mission Concept
records.description: Titan, with its dense atmosphere, dynamic ionosphere, and highly variable magnetosphere influenced by the Saturnian magnetospheric environment, presents one of the most complex plasma interactions in the solar system. Previous mission discoveries have clearly highlighted this complexity, challenging our current understanding and reshaping our knowledge of this outer planet moon. These findings support the idea that only future missions can assist with further digging into this side of planetary science. The Dioscuri space mission is a concept of an L-class mission with the proposed launch in 2036 arriving to the Saturnian world by mid-2040. The scientific aim of the mission will focus on Titan’s atmosphere and chemical and physical processes involved and is driven by NASA’s Decadal Survey 2023-2032 and ESA’s Voyage 2050 Cosmic Vision. The proposed payload will be presented with an emphasis on the instruments used to investigate the dynamics, structure and exchange processes of the Saturnian and Titan magnetospheres, how the Saturnian magnetosphere interacts with Titan and characterise the ionosphere-magnetosphere-atmospheric processes.

records.title: Energetic proton losses reveal Io's extended and longitudinally asymmetrical atmosphere
records.description: During the Io flybys I24, I27, and I31 (1999-2001), the Energetic Particle Detector (EPD) on the Galileo spacecraft detected areas of energetic proton losses (155 keV-1250 keV). To investigate the causes behind these depletions, we employed back-tracking particle simulations in conjunction with a specified atmospheric distribution and an MHD model of the plasma/atmosphere interaction. Our investigation focused on a confined region within two Io radii, predominantly influenced by Io's SO2 atmosphere. Our findings indicate that proton depletions observed during the Galileo flybys are influenced by charge exchange with the SO2 atmosphere, surface absorption, and the electromagnetic field configuration. In the 155-240 keV energy range, charge exchange emerges as a major or dominant loss process, depending on the flyby altitude. In the 540-1250 keV range, where charge exchange cross sections are orders of magnitude smaller, the decline in proton flux is attributed to surface absorption and perturbed electromagnetic fields diverting protons away from the detector. Comparing modeled losses with data, we discern signs of an extended atmosphere on the day/downstream side of Io, the absence of atmospheric collapse on the night/upstream side, and a more globally extended atmospheric component (> 1 Io radius). Our results underscore the significance of observing and modeling proton depletion around moons as a crucial tool for constraining our understanding of the electromagnetic field configuration around Io and the radial and longitudinal atmospheric distribution, which remains poorly understood.

Comparing modeled losses with data, we discern signs of an extended atmosphere on the day/downstream side of Io, the absence of atmospheric collapse on the night/upstream side, and a more globally extended atmospheric component (> 1 Io radius). Our results underscore the significance of observing and modeling proton depletion around moons as a crucial tool for constraining our understanding of the electromagnetic field configuration around Io and the radial and longitudinal atmospheric distribution, which remains poorly understood.

records.title: A study of Io’s sodium jets with the TRAPPIST telescopes
records.description: Since 2014, the TRAPPIST telescopes have been used to observe and monitor the neutral-sodium structures around Io, including notably the sodium jet, a transient and localised region structure of sodium emission that emanates from Io. The physical processes involved in the escape of particles – for example, how the volcanoes of Io provide directly or indirectly material to the Jovian plasma torus – are not yet fully understood, and the behaviour of the various neutral sodium structures, as intermediaries between Io’s atmosphere and the plasma torus, may help to bridge this gap. Observations were carried out over 17 nights in 2014–2015, 30 nights in 2021, and 23 nights in 2022–2023 with the TRAPPIST (TRAnsiting Planets and PlanetesImals Small Telescope) telescopes, in which particular attention was paid to the sodium jet and the quantification of its physical properties (length and brightness). It was found that these properties can vary greatly from one observation to another and independently of the position of Io in its orbit. Additionally, the delay between the detection of a strong jet and the subsequent contemporaneous brightening of the plasma torus and Io’s extended sodium nebula was too long to be understood as a simple injection of material by the jet, given the expected velocities of the jet particles, which indicates that jets do not straightforwardly contribute to the population of these two structures. We will also show the latest observations, including those concurrent to the last two Io flybys by Juno. This work also demonstrates the advantage of the on-going monitoring of Io provided by the TRAPPIST telescopes in understanding the variability of the sodium jet and presents a large corpus of jet detections against which work in related fields may compare.

records.title: Ionization of Ganymede’s atmosphere and its influence on the space environment
records.description: Measurements by Galileo and Juno revealed that Ganymede's magnetosphere is filled with plasma, strongly exceeding the Jovian upstream plasma density. Ionization of neutrals from Ganymede's O$_2$ dominated atmosphere is considered to be the source for the enhanced plasma density. Apart from photo-ionization processes electron-impact ionization is assumed to also play an important role. Photo-ionization rates are well constrained. However, estimations of the electron-impact-ionization rates depend on assumptions about electron densities and temperatures within the ionosphere that have not been measured yet. In our study, we investigate the influence of various assumptions about ionization and recombination on the space environment around Ganymede and compare the results with existing observations.

records.title: Investigations of Moon-Magnetosphere Interactions by the Europa Clipper Mission
records.description: The influence of the Jovian space environment on the Galilean moons is multifaceted, and observations of moon-magnetosphere interaction by the Europa Clipper will provide an understanding of the satellites’ interior structure and compositional makeup among others. The variability of Jupiter’s magnetic field at Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto induces electric currents within the moons’ conducting ocean layer, the magnitude of which depends on the ocean’s location, extent, and conductivity. The Galilean moons are also embedded in a flow of corotating plasma and energetic particles, which continuously impacts and sputters the surfaces to produce the moons’ atmosphere. In addition, micrometeorite impacts eject particles of the surface to wrap the moons in clouds of dust. The neutral atmospheres are readily ionized by energetic particles to produce an ionosphere, which gives rise to current systems electromagnetically connecting the moons to their host planet. The Europa Clipper mission will observe the causes and effects of Europa’s interaction with its space environment using a suite of in-situ and remote-sensing instruments, most notably the Europa Clipper Magnetometer (ECM), the Plasma Instrument for Magnetic Sounding (PIMS), the MAss Spectrometer for Planetary Exploration (MASPEX), the SUrface Dust Analyzer (SUDA), and the Europa Ultraviolet Spectrograph (Europa-UVS). Supporting, engineering-grade measurements will be provided by the Radiation Monitor. While the Europa Clipper mission is primarily dedicated to the exploration of Europa, some instruments will collect data continuously throughout the tour including during flybys of Ganymede and Callisto. Observations by Europa Clipper combined with complementary data acquired by JUICE are expected to provide a comprehensive picture of the interaction of the Galilean moons with Jupiter’s magnetosphere. We present the highlights of the moon-magnetosphere interaction science we seek to unravel with the Europa Clipper mission, the primary investigations involved in these studies, and joint observation opportunities with the JUICE mission.

records.title: Three-dimensional modelling of Ganymede’s Chapman-Ferraro magnetic field: A dominant excitation source for subsurface ocean induction at half Jovian synodic period.
records.description: In April 2023, the JUpiter ICy moon Explorer (JUICE) was launched en route to orbit Jupiter’s largest and only magnetic moon, Ganymede. A primary objective of JUICE aims to verify existence of the moon’s subsurface ocean and measure its responses to surrounding magnetic excitations, which will allow determination of its structure and conductivity. Excitations occur when Ganymede experiences magnetic variations at regular periods. Known examples include at Ganymede’s orbital period due to its eccentric orbit around Jupiter, and at Jovian synodic period due to the planet’s tilted dipole axis as it rotates. Excitation at half Jovian synodic period has also been considered, thought to arise from variation of Jupiter’s quadrupolar field. Because Ganymede possesses its own magnetic field, however, the magnetic gradient at Ganymede-Jupiter magnetopause generates the Chapman-Ferraro (C-F) magnetic field, which also varies at half Jovian synodic period due to variation in Jovian plasma sheet conditions. Here we present a three-dimensional analytical model of the C-F field experienced by Ganymede and demonstrate that the C-F field will dominate half Jovian synodic excitation over the Jovian quadrupolar field. Obtained analytical model results are compared to Galileo observations and results from numerical magnetohydrodynamic models to establish their validity. The C-F magnetic field therefore must be taken into account when modelling magnetic response of Ganymede’s subsurface ocean, and the half Jovian synodic induction frequency may be more exploitable than previously thought as JUICE continues its journey toward the moon.

records.title: Observed Vs. Modeled Electron Densities in Titan’s Ionosphere
records.description: Titan has a chemically complex atmosphere that ionizes to form a complicated ionosphere. The ionosphere consists of several species such as electrons, H+, CH4+, N2+ and several heavy hydrocarbon ions. In-situ observations by the Cassini spacecraft have led to a significant advancement of our understanding of Titan’s ionosphere. However, the electron densities calculated by various models below ~1200 km altitude are typically larger than those observed by Cassini. Many have tried to address this discrepancy, as a chemistry issue. While incomplete chemistry schemes are a likely candidate, there are however, other suspects that need examination. We first examine the idea that some underlying asymmetric 3-d structures and processes leads to the density discrepancies. Then we examine what role dynamics due to the interaction of Titan’s ionosphere with Saturn’s magnetosphere may play.

records.title: Electron temperature in Europa's space environment
records.description: The far ultraviolet emissions from Europa's atmosphere have been observed in many instances by the Hubble Space Telescope. These observation have given insight into Europa's atmosphere and plasma environment. Especially prominent is the OI1356 oxygen line that has been used to constrain Europa's oxygen atmosphere. Observations suggest that the hemisphere of Europa facing the dense plasma sheet is brighter. To investigate the reason behind this asymmetry we conducted a study of the plasma environment around Europa. The distribution and brightness of the far ultraviolet emission depends on the atmospheric density and the electron density and temperature. In our study, we focus on the electron environment around Europa, since we do not expect the asymmetries in Europa's neutral atmosphere to have an influence that is significant enough to produce the observed emission patterns. Therefore, we carried out simulations that solve the ideal magnetohydrodynamic equations and added an equation for the electron temperature. From that we derived the atmospheric emissions of the OI1356 oxygen line and compared to the HST observations. In our study, the electrons are cooled by non-elastic collisions with atmospheric oxygen and reheated by conductive heating along the magnetic field lines. The plasma sheet acts as reservoir for thermal energy that leads to asymmetric heating of the electrons in Europa's vicinity. The calculated images of the far ultraviolet emissions show asymmetries that are comparable to the HST observations.

records.title: Sub-surface oceans: Effects on moon-magnetosphere interaction and related implications for ocean diagnostics
records.description: The moons of Jupiter are exposed to time-variable magnetic fields primarily due to the tilt of Jupiter's magnetic moment. Therefore, electrically conductive sub-surface oceans induce secondary magnetic fields which are in the simplest description dipole magnetic fields outside of the moons. In our presentation we will discuss how the external moon-plasma interaction modifies ocean-induced fields and vice versa. We also review in-situ and remote-sensing possibilties to diagnose properties of the oceans and how these are affected by the non-linear coupling of the ocean-induced fields and the plasma interaction.

records.title: Magnetospheric impacts on and at Earth’s Moon
records.description: Every month, when we look up to the night sky and see a full moon, we can be quite certain that the Moon lies within Earth’s magnetotail, the extended portion of the anti-sunward magnetosphere that is elongated and drawn out by the solar wind. During its 27-day orbit, the Moon spends about 4-days transiting Earth’s magnetotail, where it is embedded within hot, tenuous magnetospheric plasma and an enhanced, yet time- and activity-dependent radiation and charging environment. Here, we present a very brief introduction and overview of the Moon in Earth’s magnetosphere, including details of the lunar wake and magnetotail activity, such as substorms, plasmoids, plasma flow bursts, and intense and explosive enhancements of relativistic electrons. We present results from a series of ongoing, detailed statistical studies, several of which incorporate aspects of machine learning, to better characterize the impacts of Earth’s magnetospheric activity on the lunar environment. We next go on to describe the space weather impacts, consequences, and consideration of these phenomena at the Moon, particularly from the perspective of human spaceflight and the American endeavor to return to the Moon with the Artemis program.

records.title: JUPT: A new open-source plotting tool for Juno
records.description: We present the Juno Universal Plotting Tool (JUPT), a new plotting tool to create publication ready plots of data from the Juno spacecraft. This Juno data plotting tool is the first open source tool to make the comparison between data from different instruments including a magnetometer (MAG), plasma (JADE), energetic particle (JEDI), and radio wave (Waves) instruments. Our flexible tool allows for the creation of multi-panel plots through the automatic sourcing and plotting of data and accompanying spacecraft ephemeris information. The tool can be used to plot any individual case study events. We showcase an example plot created for a flyby of Ganymede (G34) showing MAG, JADE, JEDI, Waves, and ephemeris data between UTC 2021-06-07 16:35 and UTC 2021-06-07 17:15. This work aims to show the advantages of having user-friendly generalised tools in space physics, allowing researchers to spend less time on data visualisation and more time on science. Moreover, at the core of our work is advocating for open source software and broad sharing of community tools, and thus we illustrate this through our effective use of GitHub for curating and sharing our work.

records.title: Ion cyclotron waves at Io: Pick-up rate and outgassing
records.description: With its extended mission, JUNO is getting close to Io and performs moon flybys. It is therefore time to (re)analyse the already available magnetometer data from close flybys of Io by Galileo. Earlier studies of the J0 flyby showed the presence of ion cyclotron waves generated by the pick-up of SO2+ and determined the density of the picked-up ions. In this presentation we study all five Io flybys by Galileo and investigate the presence of ion cyclotron waves for three different species. SO2+, SO+ and S+. Through Fourier analysis and calculation of the cross-spectral matrix and strong criteria on power, polarization and ellipticity, we determine intervals of significant wave activity. Under the assumption of bi-spherical scattering of the pick-up ions in the velocity ring-distribution, an estimation of the pick-up ion density can be obtained. Through an assumption of the ionization frequency, this can be converted into a neutral density to obtain a value of the total neutral gas emitted per second and compare it to the usually assumed 1000 kg/s. Naturally, the five flybys will also give information about differences generated by local time, longitude and latitude.

records.title: A global magnetohydrodynamic analysis of radial interchange instability from Enceladus mass-loading and entropy bubbles in Saturn’s magnetosphere.
records.description: When characterizing Saturn’s magnetosphere, it is impossible to discount the influence of Saturn’s moon, Enceladus, on the system. Unlike with Io at Jupiter, the material ejected from Enceladus remains neutral for a large period of time and diffuses radially away from Saturn before eventually ionizing. This creates a significant departure in neutral Keplerian orbit period from Saturn’s magnetic corotational period, and the freshly-ionized material produces significant drag on the magnetic field, stretching it and driving outward radial transport in the form of Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities. The plasma continues to move outward until the magnetic tension can no longer keep the plasma attached, and the plasma gets ejected downtail in the form of plasmoids through tail reconnection. On the planetward side of this tail reconnection, low-flux tube entropy bubbles are produced which accelerate towards the inner magnetosphere on the post-midnight side of the tail, introducing significant density variations on the dawn side of Saturn’s magnetosphere that were also observed by the Cassini spacecraft. These entropy bubbles are fairly well understood in the terrestrial magnetosphere, but not in the context of the fast rotating, mass-loaded magnetosphere of Saturn. We determine the influence these injections/bubbles have on radial transport at Saturn using the Grid Agnostic MHD for Extended Research Applications (GAMERA) global magnetosphere model in conjunction with test particle simulations. We examine the force balance on these bubbles in the context of the Southwood-Kivelson stability parameter to interpret the roles of entropy and centrifugal acceleration in the radial stability of the injection bubbles in order to predict the extent of radial injection into the inner magnetosphere. We use test particles in the global magnetosphere models to investigate the role of drift physics and to better understand transport mechanisms of injections through the dayside of Saturn’s magnetosphere.

records.title: Juno SRU Surface Images of the Galilean Satellites in Jupiter-shine
records.description: Juno’s Extended Mission has expanded the scientific reach of Juno’s low-light Stellar Reference Unit (SRU) star camera to the surfaces of the Galilean satellites. Close flybys of the dark sides of Ganymede and Europa (illuminated by Jupiter-shine) have yielded high-resolution broadband visible (450-1100nm) SRU surface images that enabled significant improvements to the geomorphologic maps of these icy moons and revealed sites of potential present day surface activity on Europa (providing high quality baselines for Europa Clipper and JUICE to investigate surface change). The Mission’s close flybys of Io in December 2023 and February 2024 present additional opportunities for low-light high-resolution SRU surface imaging on the dark side of Jupiter’s volcanic moon. We discuss highlights of the SRU findings, revealed in Jupiter-shine.

records.title: Juno’s close encounters with Ganymede, Europa, and Io: a Juno-era review of moon- magnetosphere interactions with emphasis on energetic particle dynamic
records.description: Juno, now in its extended mission, expands on the discoveries it has already made around Jupiter by visiting the Jovian moons with its highly capable space physics instrumentation. Juno’s first moon encounter was Ganymede, Jupiter’s largest moon and the only known moon to generate its own internal magnetic field. During Juno’s PJ34 orbit, it traversed the mini-magnetosphere within ~103 km of the moon’s surface. Just over a year later, in its PJ45 orbit, Juno visited Jupiter’s ocean world, Europa. The spacecraft flew over the icy moon with a closest approach of ~350 km. And most recently, in December of 2023, Juno performed one of its two scheduled close flybys of Io, the most geologically active moon in the Solar System. With each moon flyby, Juno ushered in new findings about their local space environments; however, collectively Juno is providing new insights into moon-magnetosphere interactions. These insights are based on some of the following observations: wave-particle interactions over Ganymede’s polar regions; magnetic reconnection signatures at Ganymede’s upstream magnetopause; energetic ion-sounding and agyrotropy effects near Europa; and finally, field-aligned particle populations associated with Io’s Alfvén Wing. In this presentation, we provide a Juno-era review of the interactions between Jupiter’s space environment and three of the four Galilean moons. We emphasize the energetic particle observations from Juno/JEDI and the associated interpretations, and briefly highlight plasma and field measurements.

These insights are based on some of the following observations: wave-particle interactions over Ganymede’s polar regions; magnetic reconnection signatures at Ganymede’s upstream magnetopause; energetic ion-sounding and agyrotropy effects near Europa; and finally, field-aligned particle populations associated with Io’s Alfvén Wing. In this presentation, we provide a Juno-era review of the interactions between Jupiter’s space environment and three of the four Galilean moons. We emphasize the energetic particle observations from Juno/JEDI and the associated interpretations, and briefly highlight plasma and field measurements.

records.title: JUICE: A European Mission to Jupiter and its Icy Moons
records.description: JUICE - JUpiter ICy moons Explorer - is the first large mission in the ESA Cosmic Vision program. The spacecraft was successfully launched in April 2023, and will arrive at Jupiter in 2031. It will spend about four years characterizing the Jovian system, the planet, its giant magnetosphere, and the icy Galilean moons before entering in orbit around the planet’s largest moon Ganymede for nine months. The focus of Juice is to characterize the conditions that may have led to the emergence of habitable environments among the Jovian icy satellites, with special emphasis on the three worlds, Ganymede, Europa, and Callisto, likely hosting internal oceans. The spacecraft payload consists of 10 state-of-the-art instruments (and one experiment that use the spacecraft telecommunication system with ground-based instruments) that will perform remote and in-situ measurements of Jupiter, its moons and their environment. The advanced instrumentation will permit new studies of Jupiter’s magnetosphere and its complex interaction with the Galilean satellites, to further enhance our understanding of the evolution and dynamics of the Jovian system. In December 2034, Juice will enter in orbit around Ganymede, then becoming the first orbiter of a moon that is not our own. Ganymede is identified as a high-priority target as it provides a unique laboratory for analyzing the nature, evolution and potential habitability of icy worlds, including the characteristics of subsurface oceans, and its unique magnetosphere interaction with the Jovian magnetodisc. The science objectives of the mission, its status and future plans are presented.

records.title: UV signatures of surface processing in ratioed reflectance spectra of Jupiter’s icy moons
records.description: The surfaces of Jupiter’s icy moons appear darker than expected at far- to mid-UV wavelengths (~170 – 300 nm), where water ice is highly reflective. This darkening effect is thought to be related to the magnetospheric environment in which the satellites orbit. Charged particle impact may alter the reflectance of the icy surfaces through various processes including damage to the ice lattice, production of UV-absorbing radiolysis products or lag layers, and implantation of impurities. All three icy Jovian satellites have relatively featureless UV reflectance spectra with gradual red slopes at wavelengths >165 nm but no obvious signatures of specific materials, making it difficult to determine the exact darkening mechanisms in effect. However, by ratioing reflectance spectra obtained in different locations we can identify subtle spectral differences, helping to constrain variations in surface composition potentially related to radiolytic surface processing. We present ratioed UV reflectance spectra obtained by the Hubble Space Telescope, showing relatively unprocessed water ice on Callisto’s leading hemisphere, as well as absorption features near 185 nm on Europa and near 220 nm on Ganymede. We also show disk-resolved UV ratio maps obtained by Juno-UVS during the 2021 Ganymede flyby, finding spectral differences between the icy high latitudes and ice-rich craters at lower latitudes. Finally, we discuss prospects for future mapping of radiolysis products and other non-ice materials by JUICE-UVS and Europa-UVS.

records.title: Radiation environment of the Galilean Satellites
records.description: Since its orbital insertion on July 4, 2016, the Juno spacecraft has been flying in a highly elliptical orbit around Jupiter. This orbit progressively shifts Juno's line of apsides, aligning it more closely with regions of increased particle fluxes in Jupiter's magnetic equator. These particle fluxes are continuously monitored by the micro Advanced Stellar Compass (μASC), which serves as an attitude reference for the Juno Magnetic Field Investigation. The shielding of the μASC camera head unit is designed to block electrons with energies below 15 MeV. This feature enables the μASC to function as an energetic particle sensor by detecting and recording particles that penetrate the shielding and deposit energy in the CCD sensor. Over the course of the first 57 orbits, the μASC has gathered comprehensive in-situ measurements of high-energy particle fluxes. These measurements span from regions near open field lines to the M-shell of Io, offering extensive coverage of the flux environment around the orbits of Ganymede, Europa, and Io. This presentation will focus on the interactions of highly energetic electrons with Ganymede’s magnetic field and will detail the magnitude and extent of flux variations associated with the moons Ganymede, Europa, and Io. Through this data, we aim to enhance the understanding of Jupiter's magnetosphere and the impact of its moons on particle dynamics.

records.title: A New Molecular Beam Facility for Instrument Calibration
records.description: We will present the design and establishment of a cutting-edge molecular beam facility at Southwest Research Institute (SwRI). The beam is capable of generating neutrals to 4.5 km/s in a 10-8 mbar or less environment, with a flux of 10^14 cm-2s-1. The immediate focus of this facility is to support the operations of Strofio, the neutral mass spectrometer and payload of the BepiColombo mission to Mercury. The primary goal of Strofio is to identify and characterize the chemical composition of the Hermean exosphere. By utilizing the neutral beam, we can replicate the environment of Mercury and optimize the system before arrival. Beyond serving the needs of Strofio, our vision extends to collaborative efforts with other organizations in the development of future instrumentation. We look forward to fostering partnerships that will collectively advance the capabilities of in-situ particle instruments and contribute to the broader scientific community.

records.title: Energetic particle measurements near Ganymede: Galileo EPD data revisited and perspectives for Juice PEP
records.description: The Galileo spacecraft performed close flybys of the moon Ganymede between 1996 and 2001. We reanalysed data of the energetic particles detector EPD onboard Galileo and derived the particle fluxes, energy spectra, and pitch angle distributions in the energy range of several keV to MeV during Ganymede flybys G2, G7, G8, G28, and G29. We find sharp dropouts in ion and electron fluxes as signatures of the loss cones inside the Ganymede magnetosphere as well as trapped electron distribution. Additionally, bi-directional field-aligned and butterfly distributions were found as well. We discuss these findings compared with simulation results in charactering Ganymede’s magnetosphere and in the context of future measurements with the Particle Environment Package PEP onboard the Juice mission which will be in orbit around Ganymede in 2032.

records.title: What causes transient changes in the neutral clouds and plasma torus?
records.description: Since the flybys by the Voyager missions in 1979, the moon Io is known to be extremely volcanically active as well as the to be the main source of plasma in the vast magnetosphere of Jupiter. Most of the time the magnetospheric plasma environment of Io is stable on timescales from days to months. Various observations suggest that occasionally (roughly 1-2 times per decade) the plasma torus undergoes transient changes over several weeks, apparently overcoming any stabilizing mechanisms. Such events are commonly explained by some kind of change of Io’s volcanic activity that triggers a chain of reactions changing the plasma torus state via a net increase in mass supply. A change in the neutral cloud in Io’s orbit, through which the majority of the mass transfer likely happens, was observed simultaneously with a plasma torus event in 2015, supporting this hypothesis. However, it remains unknown what kind of volcanic event(s) this might be, whether the atmosphere undergoes a general change before/during such events, and what processes could enable such a change in the otherwise stable system. We review the current knowledge on Io’s volcanic activity, atmosphere and the magnetospheric neutral and plasma environment in view of their roles in the mass transfer from Io to the plasma torus and magnetosphere.

records.title: Degenerate induced magnetospheres: lessons for the moon – magnetosphere interactions at the outer planets
records.description: Induced magnetospheres of non-magnetized atmospheric planets like Mars and Venus are formed by magnetic fields of ionospheric currents driven by the convective electric field E = - V x B/c of the solar wind. When the interplanetary magnetic field is mostly radial (the cone angle is lower than 10°-15°), the convective electric field is small, the ambipolar electric fields start playing a large role, and the induced magnetosphere degenerates. The structure of degenerate induced magnetospheres is very much different from the classical case of large cone angles and they present a specific class of the interaction with the ambient plasma flow. The conditions somewhat similar to the degenerate induced magnetospheres may occur at Uranus and Neptune. In this talk we first explain the basic physics of such structures at non-magnetized planets. We then consider what we can learn for the moon-magnetosphere interactions at the icy giants by showing results of the hybrid simulations of the Triton – Neptune magnetosphere interactions.

records.title: Pickup ions from the atmospheres of Io, Europa, and Ganymede
records.description: Juno recently performed close flybys of Io, Europa, and Ganymede, providing unprecedented plasma composition measurements with JADE, the Jovian Auroral Distributions Experiment. We will summarize the pickup ion composition observations from Juno’s satellite flybys, providing comparisons of the three innermost Galilean moons. These recent Juno observations provide new insights on the evolution of the surfaces and atmospheres of these bodies. At the icy moons, we will provide direct constraints on the radiolytic production of hydrogen and oxygen, as well as their subsequent losses from these bodies, and compare these to model expectations. At Io, we will discuss the extent to which we may constrain the loss of sulfur and oxygen from its surface and atmosphere given the specifics of the Juno flyby geometry and observations in this intense region. Finally, we will discuss how the Galilean moons interact with their plasma environments, providing sources of pickup-ions to the Jovian magnetosphere and highlight how these interactions provide analogues for satellite-moon interactions applicable to other planetary systems.

records.title: Modelling the dynamics of Io's Interaction with the Io Plasma Torus
records.description: Io presents a unique case of magnetospheric plasma interacting with a tenuous atmosphere. Its tidal heating makes Io extremely volcanically active, contributing to its SO2 atmosphere [1],[2]. This atmosphere is also influenced by SO2 surface frost, which sublimates in sunlight and re-condenses at night or during eclipse. The exact dynamics of how volcanism and sublimation combine to sustain Io's atmosphere remain unclear [3]. Further, the atmosphere is partially ionized and feeds into Jupiter's magnetosphere, forming the Io Plasma Torus. This plasma, moving faster than Io's orbital velocity, constantly interacts with Io's atmosphere. This has motivated us to investigate an approach to modelling Io’s atmosphere and provide a better understanding of the ongoing dynamic processes. Our model is based on previous simulations of plumes [4], the sublimation atmosphere [5] and plasma heating [6]. For the calculation of the gas flow, we apply the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method [7], ideal for handling the varying gas densities on Io. Further, we can incorporate dust particles, using the DRAG3D code [8],[9] to simulate dust movement based on the gas flow results. This allows us to explore various dust sizes and properties, aiding in creating synthetic images of dust density and reflectance. We aim to present simulation results of various scenarios combining sublimation, volcanic activity, and plasma interactions to deepen our understanding of these processes. This research is particularly relevant considering upcoming missions like JUICE, Europa Clipper, and a possible future Io Volcano Observer. References: [1] Tsang, C. et al. (2015). [2] Spencer, J.R. et al. (2005). [3] de Pater, I. et al. (2021). [4] McDoniel, W. et al. (2019). [5| Walker, A. et al. (2010). [6] Moore, C.H. et al. (2011). [7] Bird, G.A. (1994). [8] Marschall, R. et al. (2016). [9] Gerig, S. et al. (2020).

records.title: The roles of flux-tube entropy and effective gravity in the inward plasma transport at Saturn
records.description: The inward plasma transport at Saturnian magnetosphere is examined using the flux tube interchange stability formalism developed by Southwood and Kivelson (1987). Seven events are selected. Three cases are considered: (1) the injected flux-tube and ambient plasmas are nonisotropic; (2) the injected flux-tube and ambient plasmas are isotropic and (3) the injected flux-tube plasma is isotropic but the ambient plasma is nonisotropic. Case (1) may be relevant for fresh injections while case (3) may be relevant for old injections. For cases (1) and (2), all but one events have negative stability condition, suggesting that the flux-tube should be moving inward. For case (3), the injections located at L > 11 have negative stability condition, while 4 out of 5 of the injections at L < 9 have positive stability condition. The positive stability condition for small L suggests that the injection may be near its equilibrium position and possibly oscillating thereabouts---hence the outward transport if the flux tube overshot the equilibrium position. The flux-tube entropy plays an important role in braking the plasma inward transport. When the stability condition is positive, it is because the entropy term, which is positive, counters and dominates the effective gravity term, which is negative for all the events. The ambient plasma and drift out from adjacent injections can affect the stability and the inward motion of the injected flux tube. The results have implications to inward plasma transport in Jovian magnetosphere as well as other fast rotating planetary magnetospheres. The effect of Enceladus on the plasma injection is discussed.

records.title: Ganymede's oxygen and water atmosphere during eclipse passage
records.description: Ganymede possess a global O$_2$ atmosphere. Only near the sub-solar point the density of sublimated H$_2$O might prevail. This H$_2$O component likely condenses at night as well as during eclipse, when the surface temperature is expected to drop significantly. In December 2023, the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) obtained UV images of auroral emissions from Ganymede while the moon was eclipsed by Jupiter as well as directly after egress from eclipse. Ganymede's auroral emissions are excited when electrons collide atmospheric neutrals and thereby produce excited oxygen atoms. The HST images show auroral oxygen emissions around two wavelengths (1304 Å and 1356 Å) and the relative brightness of these depends primarily on the neutral species. By comparing the emission images at 1304 Å and 1356 Å we infer the relative abundance of O$_2$, O and H$_2$O around Ganymede in and after eclipse.

records.title: Resonant Acceleration of Electrons and Protons Driven by Satellite-Magnetosphere Interactions
records.description: The Juno spacecraft has frequently transited through magnetic flux tubes connected to the innermost three Galilean satellites - Io, Europa, and Ganymede, and their wakes, during which it has typically observed higher particle fluxes and plasma wave activity. We present new observations of proton and electron distributions observed by the JADE instrument during these intervals which exhibit banded structures in energy. The energies corresponding to the banded flux enhancements are linearly spaced in particle speed, suggesting a link between the observed structure and a resonant wave-particle interaction operating at those energies with the wave and its harmonics. We show that the bounce periods for both protons and electrons at the orbits of the Galilean moons are of similar order as eigenperiods of standing Alfvén waves in the form of field line resonances (FLRs). The observations demonstrate that the Galilean moons can excite field-line resonances via their interaction with the Jovian magnetospheric plasma and that resonant wave-particle interaction can occur at lower frequencies between these standing waves and the bounce motion of the particles.

records.title: Overview of Juno Plasma Wave Observations at Ganymede, Europa, and Io
records.description: The Juno extended mission at Jupiter has enabled close flybys of Ganymede, Europa, and Io, providing a temporal link between the observations by Galileo and the anticipated JUICE and Europa Clipper missions. And, Juno provides enhancements in instrumental capabilities from those of Galileo. Here, we provide an overview of the plasma wave spectra near these moons and what they can tell us about their interactions with the surrounding Jovian magnetosphere. In each case, the waves show aspects of electromagnetic links to Jupiter via its magnetic field. These include evidence of electron beams and hints of reconnection such as at Ganymede’s magnetopause. Wave-particle interactions primarily involving whistler mode waves such as chorus are also evident, particularly in the complex magnetosphere-magnetosphere interaction at Ganymede, but at Europa, as well. Low-frequency waves including electrostatic solitary waves are apparent at each moon. Plasma waves can also provide a means of determining the electron density in and near the interaction region. In some cases the electric field waveforms provide evidence of the dust environment and we summarize those observations, as well.

records.title: Modeling the neutral and ionized environments of Callisto
records.description: Callisto is the most distant of the four Galilean moons, orbiting at a distance of 26.3 Jovian radii from its planet. Composed of rock and ice in similar quantities, the moon has a tenuous atmosphere composed mainly of $O_2$ [Cunningham et al., 2015] and $CO_2$ [Carlson et al., 1999], as well as an ionosphere characterized by densities of up to $10^4\ cm^{-3}$, but only when the trailing hemisphere is illuminated by the Sun [Kliore et al., 2002]. NASA's Galileo mission detected an induced magnetic field that could be indirect evidence of the existence of a subsurface ocean in the moon's interior. Callisto's environment interacts with Jupiter's magnetosphere, in which it is embedded, leading to erosion of the moon's surface and the formation of Alfvén waves. In addition, Callisto's orbital environment is highly variable due to its rapid excursion in magnetic latitude as Jupiter rotates. The interaction between Callisto's plasma and neutral environment and the Jovian magnetosphere is still not fully understood. Therefore, as part of the JUICE mission, which will include several flybys of Callisto, simulations describing the moons' neutral and ionized environments must be carried out. These simulations will be done using the LatHyS generic multi-species parallel 3D model [Modolo et al., 2016; 2018] and the EGM generic multi-species 3D exospheric model [Leblanc et al., 2017; Oza et al., 2019]. Due to the characteristics of the system under study, an MHD approach cannot be realized and a "hybrid" formalism has to be used, with ions represented by numerical macro-particles and electrons by an inertial-free fluid, both coupled through Maxwell's equations. Simulation results will be analyzed and validated in comparison with data from previous in situ missions (Galileo, Juno) and observations from Earth (HST). In parallel, data from the Juno mission will be used to characterize the moon's orbital environment.

records.title: Juno/JADE plasma observations during the Ganymede flyby
records.description: We present Juno/JADE plasma observations during Juno's flyby of Ganymede. On June 7, 2021, ~20 years after the last Galileo flyby, the Juno spacecraft flew by Ganymede and briefly entered its magnetosphere. Juno carried the Jovian Auroral Distributions Experiment (JADE), which measured electron (0.32-32 keV) and ion (0.013-46 keV/q) distributions. Plasma disturbances were observed well before Juno entered Ganymede’s magnetosphere and were followed by an excursion into a region of Ganymede’s wake environment that had not been observed by Galileo [1]. In Ganymede’s wake, a weak and turbulent magnetic field was correlated with unexpectedly dense, heated plasma with broad angular distribution. Juno then crossed into Ganymede’s magnetosphere, where JADE observed cold, outflowing ionospheric ions O2+, O+, H2+, H+, and H3+ [2]. As Juno exited Ganymede’s magnetosphere, JADE measured accelerated, field-aligned electron distributions indicative of magnetic reconnection [3]. In this presentation, we give an overview of JADE observations during Juno’s Ganymede flyby and highlight new findings that enhance our present understanding of Ganymede’s magnetosphere, such as the unexpected observation of H3+ and the presence of the previously unexplored wake region. records.title: Origin of Ganymede's polar caps
records.description: Hemispherical differences in the spectral properties of icy satellites are known to be related to interactions with the magnetospheres of their parent planet. This interaction is even more complex in case of Ganymede. In addition to hemispherical differences, Ganymede’s polar regions experience an enhanced impact of charged particles originating from the Jovian magnetosphere (Khurana et al. 2007, Icarus, 191). This interaction is believed to form Ganymede’s thin polar caps visible in the images of the cameras active during the Voyager and Galileo missions. However, detailed analyses of the data provided by Galileo NIMS revealed that water ice grain sizes continuously decrease with increasing latitude with the same trend and that the same trend can be observed on the neighboring satellite Callisto, which does not exhibit a magnetic field like Ganymede (Stephan et al. 2020, Icarus, 337). Thus, both trends should result from the same process favoring diurnal variations in the surface temperature causing the continuous sublimation, migration and redeposition of water ice into colder northern regions. Small-grained water ice (< 1μm) combined with a generally higher abundance of water ice on Ganymede’s surface can explain the appearance of Ganymede’s polar caps (Stephan et al. 2021, Minerals, 11). A detailed mapping and monitoring of radiation products in the polar region down to the region where Ganymede’s closed magnetic field lines change into open ones (~ 40° lat) can prove the interaction of the surface ice with magnetospheric particles. MAJIS, one of the instruments onboard the JUICE spacecraft, will enable such investigation. However, the illumination conditions in the polar regions continuously worsen during the JUICE mission (Stephan et al., 2021, PSS, 208). It is strongly recommended to start this investigation as early as possible and that the most relevant data should be collected before JUICE enters the GCO500 orbit phase.

records.title: Titan caught in the act? A surprising brief but intense period of atmospheric loss
records.description: Prior to Cassini’s arrival at Saturn, the nitrogen-rich dense unprotect atmosphere of Titan was considered a significant, if not dominant, source of heavy particles in Saturn’s magnetosphere. However, the wealth of data provided by Cassini has pointed to Enceladus as the dominant source of material in the magnetosphere in the form of water-group particles as opposed to nitrogen. This surprising insight has shown how a relatively small body can dominate an entire giant magnetosphere and has completely changed our perspective on sources, sinks and fundamental magnetospheric processes. However, more recent results are starting to indicate that Titan is actually having a (less obvious) significant impact on Saturn’s magnetosphere. Although Titan’s atmosphere is dominated by nitrogen, hydrocarbons make up about ~1.4% of the atmosphere (Coustenis and Taylor, 2008) and these species were routinely observed by INMS when Cassini entered Titan’s atmosphere. Interestingly, Westlake et al. (2012) identified an outflow of hydrocarbon carbon ions from Titan’s atmosphere at 0.8-1.5 km/s. Additionally, Woodson et al. (2014) identified hydrocarbon ions near Titan. Thus, atmospheric escape from Titan has been hypothesized as a noticeable source of carbon ions. Of particular interest for this work, a thorough analysis of Cassini data has revealed a surprising carbon ion enhancement in Saturn’s magnetosphere during 2014. For this work, we present data analysis and modeling results of this carbon ion enhancement and its implications for Titan with regard to atmospheric escape and its interaction with (and impact to) Saturn’s magnetosphere.

records.title: Particle Environment Package (PEP) for the JUICE mission: current status
records.description: Particle Environment Package (PEP) onboard ESA Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (JUICE) provides particle measurements to answer three overarching science questions: (1) How does the co-rotating magnetosphere of Jupiter interact with Ganymede, Callisto, Europa, and Io? (2) How do internal and solar wind drivers cause such energetic, time variable and multi-scale phenomena in the steadily rotating giant magnetosphere of Jupiter? (3) What are the structure and composition of the icy moons exospheres and how do they response to the external conditions? PEP measures positive and negative ions, electrons, exospheric neutral gas, thermal plasma and energetic neutral atoms (ENA) present in all domains of the Jupiter system over nine (9) decades of energy from 1 MeV with full angular coverage. The six PEP sensors are: • Jovian plasma Dynamics and Composition analyzer (JDC); • Jovian Electrons and Ions analyzer (JEI); • Jovian Energetic Electrons (JoEE); • Jovian Energetic Neutrals and Ions sensors (JENI); • Jovian Neutrals Analyzer (JNA); • Neutral gas and Ion Mass spectrometer (NIM). The PEP sensors are grouped into two groups PEP-Lo (JDC, JEI, JNA, NIM) and PEP-Hi (JENI, JoEE) covering well overlapping energy ranges up to 10s keV and up to 1 MeV respectively. For the first time at Jupiter PEP combines magnetospheric ENA imaging with in-situ measurements and performs remote sensing via ENAs of the Europa/Io tori. Using low energy ENAs originating from the particle – surface interaction PEP investigates space weathering of the icy moons by precipitation particles. PEP will directly sample the exospheres of Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto with never achieved before mass resolution > 700. JUICE successfully launched on 14 April, 2023. PEP-Hi is fully commissioned. JEI and JDC plan to be fully commissioned by the Moon-Earth fly-by in August 2024.

records.title: Plasma interaction with the Moon is not boring
records.description: Unlike previous thoughts, observations over the last two decades have proven that the Earth's Moon is not a boring object for space physics, and the plasma interaction with the Moon is indeed complex and rich in fundamental plasma physics. Despite lacking a global intrinsic magnetic field and a dense atmosphere, the Moon engages in a fascinating interplay with solar wind plasma due to its small-scale crustal magnetic fields. This interaction occurs at sub-ion inertial length scales, where kinetic processes play a crucial role. Approximately 75% of the Moon's orbital path occurs in the solar wind, while the remaining 25% takes place within the Earth's magnetosphere. During its exposure to the solar wind, the Moon interacts with super magnetosonic plasma, whereas within the magnetosphere, the interaction is subsonic and sub-Alfvenic. In this comprehensive review, we summarize plasma interaction with the Moon and put it into a comparative context with similar processes occurring at the moons of outer planets. The fascinating journey of ESA's JUICE mission to Jupiter will include a Moon flyby scheduled for August 2024.

records.title: Probing the Subsurface of Io, Europa and Ganymede with Juno’s Microwave Radiometer
records.description: On June 7, 2021, and September 29, 2022, the NASA Juno spacecraft passed Jupiter’s Galilean moons, Ganymede, and Europa, respectively. The closest approach distance was only ~1000 km above Ganymede, and only ~350 km above Europa. More recently, on December 30, 2023 Juno passed by Io at a distance of 1500 km and is planned do so a second time on February 3, 2024 at a similar distance. The close flybys were the first encounters with the moons in over two decades and provided the first opportunity to map the subsurface of the their shells at multiple microwave frequencies using Juno’s Microwave Radiometer (MWR). The observations provided several swaths across the moons at six frequencies, ranging from 600 MHz to 22 GHz. The ice transparency at microwave frequencies is dependent on purity; assuming pure ice, the observations probe depths ranging from meters to kilometers. The MWR observations represent the first resolved interrogation of Ganymede and Europa’s subsurface ice shell revealing new constraints on porosity, fracturing, differences in terrain type and possibly the thickness of the ice shell. These unprecedented measurements of Io, Europa and Ganymede will allow comparative studies of the surfaces and subsurface structures of the Jovian satellites. The Juno MWR measurements complement previous ground-based radar and microwave radiometry observations, which provided early characterization of these surfaces. Moon- magnetosphere interactions affect both the interpretation of radiometric signals on the surface and at depth. A comparison of the microwave spectra for all three satellites will be presented, as well as a detailed analysis and interpretation of the MWR data that provide new constraints on ice subsurface properties.

records.title: Wave-particle interactions associated with Io: A Juno overview
records.description: The Juno spacecraft crosses high-latitude magnetic flux tubes connected to Io’s orbit at least once in each hemisphere during every orbit. Additionally, Juno is scheduled to perform two Io flybys at an altitude of 1,500 km. Altogether, these provide unprecedented spatial coverage enabling (non-simultaneous) multi-point measurements along and downtail of the Main Alfvén Wing. This allows for the most complete experimental investigation of Io’s electrodynamic interaction with Jupiter’s magnetosphere/ionosphere to date. Using Juno’s high-resolution fields and particles payload, we present an overview of the types and roles of MHD and plasma waves measured across fluid, ion, and electron scales. Further, we present possible pathways that couple the observed waves to the charged particles’ energies and pitch angles. Finally, we present compelling evidence of Alfvén wave filamentation, originally hypothesized during the Galileo era, by constraining the acceleration efficiency, i.e., the fraction of Alfvénic Poynting flux that goes into electron energy flux in the loss cone.

records.title: Surface charging of JUICE in the solar wind at 1 AU
records.description: We present a study of the interaction between the Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (JUICE) spacecraft and the solar wind environment at 1 AU. The state-of-the-art software Spacecraft Plasma Interaction Software (SPIS) was used to simulate the surface charging of the spacecraft and the altered particle environment around the spacecraft. The simulations show that for a typical solar wind environment the spacecraft will charge to around 9 V, with the different dielectric parts of the spacecraft charging to potentials from around -42 to 12 V. For the extreme solar wind environment, such as the one found in the sheath region inside the shock front of an Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejection (ICME), the spacecraft charges more negatively due to the increased accumulation of electrons. In this environment, the spacecraft charges to around 3 V, with the different dielectric surfaces charging from around -30 to 8 V. We also show how the interaction between the spacecraft and its environment alters the ion and electron particle environment around the spacecraft. The results from this study will be used to correct the JUICE charged particle and field measurements for the impact of the spacecraft - plasma interaction.

records.title: Structure and dynamics of the Io Plasma Torus: from multi-spacecraft and multi-instrument observations to models
records.description: A number of spacecraft have flown by Jupiter or have been put into orbit around the planet. Some of them crossed the Io Plasma Torus, which is the main source of charged particles for the magnetosphere of Jupiter. We use publicly available plasma data obtained by the Voyager, Galileo, and Juno (up to PJ 50) in order to describe the radial, latitudinal, longitudinal and local time variations of the plasma moments in the torus. We also search for signatures of dynamical events connected to plasma transport through the interchange instability mechanism. We will finally present a new simplified mathematical model of the Io torus aimed at describing the links between generation and loss mechanisms of the atmosphere and neutral cloud, chemical processes, torus ions pickup and plasma exchange with the magnetodisk, which will assimilate observational data in the model. We will discuss our preliminary modeling results and their implications on the role of the Io source on Jovian magnetosphere dynamics.

records.title: Latitudinal and Longitudinal Structure of Io's Atmosphere Explained by a Purely Sublimation Driven Atmosphere
records.description: How much Io's SO$_2$ atmosphere is driven by direct volcanic outgasing or the sublimation of SO$_2$ surface frost is a question with a considerable history. In our work we develop a time dependent surface temperature model including the effect of thermal inertia. Analyzing the conductive heat transfer from Io's surface towards its interior and vice versa, which is mainly determined by the thermal conductivity $\kappa$, allows us to show that many observations can be explained by assuming a purely sublimation driven atmosphere. Simulations show that $\kappa=0.62$ Wm$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ yields an averaged atmospheric SO$_2$ column density decreasing by more than one order of magnitude from the equator to the poles. In a parameter study regarding the thermal inertia we find that a thermal conductivity lower by a factor of 12 results in an atmosphere having both features, a less pronounced latitudinal dependence but a strong day-night asymmetry. Investigating Io's sub-anti-Jovian hemisphere asymmetry, we find maximum dayside column densities of $2\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-2}$ for the sub-Jovian and $\sim10^{17}$ cm$^{-2}$ for the anti-Jovian hemisphere. Looking at diurnal variations, we find the skin depth to be 0.7 m. Furthermore we quantify seasonal effects of the atmosphere, with Io having a northern summer close to Perihelion and a northern winter close to Aphelion. Finally, we found that an internal heat flux higher by a factor of 3 in the polar regions would explain Io's poles to be hotter in observations than resulting from modeling with an effective internal heat flow of 0.48 Wm$^{-2}$.

search_fields.title: Latitudinal and Longitudinal Structure of Io's Atmosphere Explained by a Purely Sublimation Driven Atmosphere
search_fields.description: How much Io's SO$_2$ atmosphere is driven by direct volcanic outgasing or the sublimation of SO$_2$ surface frost is a question with a considerable history. In our work we develop a time dependent surface temperature model including the effect of thermal inertia. Analyzing the conductive heat transfer from Io's surface towards its interior and vice versa, which is mainly determined by the thermal conductivity $\kappa$, allows us to show that many observations can be explained by assuming a purely sublimation driven atmosphere. Simulations show that $\kappa=0.62$ Wm$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ yields an averaged atmospheric SO$_2$ column density decreasing by more than one order of magnitude from the equator to the poles. In a parameter study regarding the thermal inertia we find that a thermal conductivity lower by a factor of 12 results in an atmosphere having both features, a less pronounced latitudinal dependence but a strong day-night asymmetry. Investigating Io's sub-anti-Jovian hemisphere asymmetry, we find maximum dayside column densities of $2\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-2}$ for the sub-Jovian and $\sim10^{17}$ cm$^{-2}$ for the anti-Jovian hemisphere. Looking at diurnal variations, we find the skin depth to be 0.7 m. Furthermore we quantify seasonal effects of the atmosphere, with Io having a northern summer close to Perihelion and a northern winter close to Aphelion. Finally, we found that an internal heat flux higher by a factor of 3 in the polar regions would explain Io's poles to be hotter in observations than resulting from modeling with an effective internal heat flow of 0.48 Wm$^{-2}$.

records.title: The Neptune-Odyssey mission
records.description: The Neptune-Odyssey mission concept (1) is a flagship-class orbiter and probe to the Neptune-Triton system developed in 2020 for NASA’s decadal survey (2). The presence of the planet-sized moon, Triton (a captured dwarf planet from the Kuiper Belt and a geophysically re-activated twin of Pluto) lead to Neptune being scientifically favored over Uranus for a Flagship Ice Giant mission (3). Given the timing of the decadal survey and NASA’s typical development timelines Neptune-Odyssey was developed under the assumption that it would not be ready for launch in time to take advantage of Jupiter gravity assist windows which close in 2032 for both Neptune and Uranus. Instead, an SLS rocket with a Centaur upper stage (or a Falcon Heavy class vehicle using a solar electric propulsion kickstage) allows for annual direct-to-Neptune launch opportunities. The Cassini-like spacecraft would launch with 3520 kg to Neptune orbit and utilize 3 RTGs, requiring 28.8 kg of Plutonium and represents a “shovel-ready” mission with a Concept Maturity Level of 4. In our presentation we will discuss the options for humanity’s first exploration of an Ice Giant system with a focus on what might be learned from a Flagship-class mission to the Neptune system. 1 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. 2023. records.title: Trident: A template for a lower cost mission to explore the Triton-Neptune Magnetosphere Interactions
records.description: Triton, the largest of Neptune's icy moons, was the highest priority potential ocean world in the Roadmap to Ocean Worlds. Its highly inclined orbit combined with Neptune's highly asymmetric magnetosphere provides for a strongly time-variable moon-magnetosphere interaction, and the opportunity to magnetically sound its interior and characterize the putative subsurface ocean utilizing a single flyby. Triton's composition, its young surface, intense ionosphere and the presence of active plumes provide the foundation for a range of critical formation, interaction, and evolution questions that are highly relevant to a broad cross-section of the planetary community. The Trident Discovery Mission to Triton provides a template for achieving high-impact science in the outer solar system at a lower cost. Its objectives, straightforward and achievable: 1. Is Triton and ocean world? 2. What processes resurface Triton? 3. What drives Triton's plumes? 4. Why is Triton's ionosphere so intense? After Phase A selection, the Trident mission concept was highly rated, with 'Excellent' science and 'Medium' risk; definitively selectable. Such a mission concept also opens the door for a New Frontiers scale mission to consider additional science related to Neptune's magnetosphere, its atmosphere, and the overall influence of Triton on Neptune's magnetospheric composition and dynamics. In short, Triton-Neptune science is imminently achievable without a flagship budget, and the Trident mission study alone led to an explosion in papers and fundamental research in this area indicating we are even more prepared now to define a mission to this exciting system.

records.title: Applications of the Multi-Model Ensemble System for the outer Heliosphere (MMESH) to Moon Space Plasma Environments
records.description: The moons of the outer planets are immersed in a fundamentally different space plasma environment than any of the planets: within the magnetospheres of the outer planets, where plasma dynamics are dominated by the planetary rotation rate and strong internal magnetic fields. Each of these intra-magnetosphere environments differ significantly from one another as well, with magnetic dipole moments ranging over nearly three orders of magnitude and the longest rotational periods nearly double the shortest. The effects of solar wind driving on each of these magnetospheres, and therefore on each of the environments of the moons within, are expected to vary significantly between planets, ranging from a weak effect at Jupiter to a dominant effect in the warped magnetospheres of the ice giants. The nature of this relationship, however, remains poorly constrained, owing to the limitations of single-spacecraft missions, which cannot simultaneously sample both extra-magnetospheric (i.e., the upstream solar wind) and intra-magnetospheric conditions. In the absence of dedicated upstream solar wind monitors for any of the outer planets, one useful method to better characterize the effects of changing solar wind conditions on moon-magnetosphere interactions is improved statistical understanding of solar wind propagation models. Here we present a suite of analysis routines for this purpose: the Multi-Model Ensemble System for the outer Heliosphere (MMESH). MMESH allows for self-consistently quantifying uncertainties in existing solar wind propagation models, detrending of model biases, and composition of robust ensemble models with estimated uncertainties. The steps are crucial for meaningful statistical analyses of solar wind-magnetosphere, and thus solar wind-moon-environment, interactions. We will include in this discussion various potential applications of this system to the space plasma environments of the moons of the outer planets.

records.title: Moon-Atmosphere Coupling at Jupiter: Heating of Jupiter's Upper Atmosphere by Auroral Currents from Io
records.description: The auroral current system connecting the galilean moons to Jupiter results in heating of the upper atmospheres at both ends of the current loop. It is possible to measure the neutral atmosphere temperature in auroral regions at Jupiter through high resolution spectra of the H2 emission bands. The ratio of band intensities can be modeled to reveal the ro-vibrational temperature of the emitting H2. Recent observations of the northern auroral region with HST / STIS and a high resolution grating were obtained with a scan of a long, narrow aperture across the emitting area. The field of view passed across the magnetic footprint of Io and the downstream tail emission regions, with reasonable signal from the H2 Lyman and Werner band emissions. The observations and subsequent modeling of the spectra will be presented.

records.title: Plasma Environment around the Enceladus and E ring
records.description: During the thirteen years of exploration in Saturn’s magnetosphere, the Cassini conducted a total of 22 flyby of the icy moon Enceladus as well as its surrounding E ring region. The Langmuir Probe onboard Cassini, by measuring the positively and negatively charged particle density, revealed the unique plasma characteristics in the results of the charged dust and negative ions produced from the cryovolcanic geyser located at the south pole of the moon. We will discuss the dust and plasma characteristics of the Enceladus plume and associated E ring environment by re-analyzing the LP data during the Enceladus flybys.

records.title: A localized and surprising source of energetic particles in the Uranian magnetosphere near Ariel
records.description: A fresh survey of energetic particle observations from the Low Energy Charged Particle (LECP) instrument on Voyager 2 revealed a previously underappreciated signature. Specifically, LECP observed a significant (several orders of magnitude) discrepancy between the intensity of energetic particles (both ions and electrons) observed during the outbound leg of the Uranus flyby encounter in the region between Miranda and Ariel compared to the inbound leg. Of particular interest are the pitch angle distributions (PADs) measured by LECP, which display extremely steep gradients. Such a steep gradient in pitch angle is difficult to maintain since any waves would act to scatter the particles and isotropize the distribution. Maintaining such a steep PAD would require a significant and relatively constant source of energetic particles, specifically for those at near-90° pitch angles, at rates that can balance or even overcome any loss/scattering processes from waves. To assess whether such an energetic particle source is in fact present in the Uranian system, distributions of the phase space density (PSD) profiles of the ions were investigated. A clear maximum between Miranda and Ariel at L~7 suggests a source of energetic ions in this region. Potential energetic particle sources include particle injections, cosmic ray albedo neutron decay (CRAND), and an active moon (i.e., a candidate ocean world). Both particle injections and CRAND are believed to be unlikely sources. However, an active moon source is potentially plausible. First, the narrow pitch angle source required matches that expected from newly created pickup ions. Other Voyager 2 observations also provide potential additional evidence to support an active moon source. These results suggest the exciting possibility of the existence of a potential ocean world(s) in the system.
